title: The Fathers on Ecclesiastes
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The Preacher is Christ, who generates this knowledge, or the one who purifies souls through ethical teaching.
comments.comment: The Church is the true knowledge of pure souls of ages and worlds and of the judgment and providence within them. The Preacher is Christ, the generator of this knowledge; or the Preacher is the one who, through ethical theorems, purifies souls and brings them to natural contemplation.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Even the contemplation of created things is vanity of vanities before the knowledge of God, as medicines are vain once health is perfect.
comments.comment: Regarding 'vanity of vanities' (Eccl 1:2), the Preacher says, 'vanity of vanities, all things are vanity.' To those entering the intelligible Church and marveling at the contemplation of the things that have come to be, the word says: do not think this is the ultimate end reserved for you by the promises; for all these things are vanity of vanities before the knowledge of God himself. Just as medicines are vain after the perfection of health, so the discourses of ages and worlds are vain after the knowledge of the Holy Trinity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the Preacher calls all things vanity.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The 'no remembrance of the former things' will come when the mind, having received the Holy Trinity, is separated from all concepts and forgets all events.
comments.comment: Regarding 'there is no remembrance of the former things' (Eccl 1:11): if there is no remembrance of the former things, how does David say, 'I remembered days of old' (Psalm 77:5) and 'I remembered eternal years' (Psalm 77:5)? Or will the total oblivion of all these things occur whenever the rational nature receives the Holy Trinity; for then God will be all in all (1 Cor 15:28). If the concepts of things occurring in the intellect lead the mind to a remembrance of things, the mind having beheld God is separated from all concepts; therefore, the mind receiving the Holy Trinity forgets all events.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The 'evil' in the distraction means what is superfluous, not what is opposed to the good, since God is not the cause of evils.
comments.comment: Regarding 'God gave the sons of men a bad distraction' (Eccl 1:13): 'evil' refers to that which is superfluous, not that which is opposed to the good; for God gives nothing of that, for He is not the cause of evils, being a source of goodness, unless it is said He gives in the sense of forgiving according to the logic of abandonment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God can be said to give a 'bad distraction' without being the cause of evil.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A distorted mind can be adorned, but wisdom cannot adorn it further unless it cleanses itself through the virtues and becomes a useful vessel to the Master.
comments.comment:
Regarding 'being strayed, it will not be able to be adorned, and being lacking, it will not be able to be numbered' (Eccl 1:15).

Regarding the distorted, the impure mind, he says: 'for a distorted heart is made crooked by evil' (Prov 3:8). But he named wisdom as 'order' in the Proverbs, where he says: 'order is wisdom to youths' (Prov 3:21); 'therefore wisdom will not enter a craftily-evil soul' (Wisdom 1:4). Yet he did not say: it will not be able to be adorned, but: it will not be able to be adorned-upon; for life indeed adorns someone rightly, but the wisdom of God adorns-upon. Thus, indeed, a distorted mind is able to be adorned, but is not able to be adorned-upon, unless through the virtues it cleanses itself and makes itself a useful vessel to the Master.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The number of God counts the holy spirits in order, while evil's victims are countless in a way that does not fit the spiritual number, and 'countless' can mean either not countable by nature or not counted for some cause.
comments.comment:
The number of God, which counts the holy spirits as some kind and appointed order, declares: 'for of numbers, he says, multitudes of stars and names of good things for all of them' (Ps 147:4). By this number the Lord also commands Moses to count the sons of Israel (Num 1:2); but what does David say concerning the crawling men and those serving pleasures? 'There are crawlers of whom there is no number' (Psalm 104:25); and in the Proverbs Solomon says concerning evil: 'for having wounded many, it has cast down, and they are countless whom it has slain' (Proverbs 7:26). What is therefore said here is a deficiency, and the slain and the crawlers are of the same state, which does not fit the spiritual number.

And if David says also that the wisdom of God is not a number, he writes not as if its worthiness were not of the number, but as if it were not of the nature to be subjected to number because of being incomprehensible. For just as the invisible is said in two ways, and that which is not of the nature to be seen, as God, and that which is of the nature to be seen, but not being seen, as iron in the depths because of being covered by water, so also the countless is said in two ways, and that which is not of the nature to be counted, and that which is not being counted because of some cause.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He turned to a life of luxury and many pleasures, held back laughter and disciplined pleasure, and set out to see what is truly good for people in this present life.
comments.comment: Judging that this was indeed so, I resolved to turn to another way of life: to give myself over to luxury and to make trial of pleasures of many kinds (Ecclesiastes 2:1). Now I have understood that all such things are vain. I held back laughter that ran on without reason, and I disciplined pleasure into sobriety, rebuking it sharply (Ecclesiastes 2:2). And reasoning that the soul can steady the body's nature when it is drunk and flowing like wine, and that self-control makes desire its slave, I was eager to see what worthy thing is set before human beings, what is truly good, that they may accomplish in this present life (Ecclesiastes 2:3).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The soul gains knowledge by purity, not by word, and in proportion to its state, so the one who is receptive withholds nothing from the eyes.
comments.comment: … And all that my eyes desired, I did not withhold from them; I did not prevent my heart from all joy (Ecclesiastes 2:10). The soul does not seek knowledge by word, but by purity; 'for not everyone saying to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father' (Matt 7:21). For according to the proportion of the state, we receive knowledge, just as the measure by which we measure shall be measured to us. Therefore, a request is the noetic dispassion of a rational soul, drawing holy knowledge to itself. Thus, he who makes himself receptive, providing all knowledge, does not take anything away from the eyes; but I say, all knowledge that is natural, which happens to a soul bound by blood and flesh.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Whoever sins in nothing does not hold back his heart from spiritual joy, and 'spirit' here names the soul, since choice is a movement of the mind.
comments.comment: He who sins in nothing does not prevent his heart from all spiritual joy (Ecclesiastes 2:10). And behold, all is vanity and a choice of the spirit (Eccl 2:11). Spirit is what names the soul; for choice is a certain movement of the mind. And David: 'Into your hands I will commit my spirit' (Ps 31:5); and Stephen: 'Lord Jesus, says he, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59); and in the Kingdoms: 'David did not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son' (2 Samuel 13:21).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: His wisdom grew less as desire grew, until he came to his senses and saw that what he held was wretched, the works of a spirit that is not good.
comments.comment: Then it happened that my wisdom grew less, while desire that is not good increased. For I gave way to every lure of the eyes and to the unchecked impulses of the heart that pressed on me from every side (Ecclesiastes 2:10); I surrendered myself to the hope of pleasures, and I tied my own will fast to every wretched luxury. For so far had my thoughts been carried toward ruin that I believed these things were good and that it was right for me to pursue them. Then at last I came to my senses and lifted my eyes, and I saw what I had in my hands: things wretched and utterly grievous, the works of a spirit that is not good (Ecclesiastes 2:11). For now nothing at all that human beings choose appears to me, by right reason, worth accepting or worth pursuing with zeal.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the Preacher's own turning point from pleasure to sense in plain words.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Good sense and folly differ as day and night: the one who has chosen virtue walks in clear daylight, while the one entangled in wickedness strays blind as on a moonless night.
comments.comment: So, weighing together the goods of wisdom and the evils of folly, I would rightly admire, and greatly, any man who has been carried along without reason and then takes hold of himself and turns back to what he ought (Ecclesiastes 2:12). For the gap between good sense and folly is wide; the difference between them is as great as between day and night (Ecclesiastes 2:13). The one who has chosen virtue is like a man who sees each thing clearly and looks upward, and who makes his journey in the brightest daylight; but the one entangled in wickedness is like a man straying in every kind of error, as on a moonless night, blind to what lies before him and cut off by the darkness from the things around him (Ecclesiastes 2:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between wisdom and folly with the image of day and night.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Christ is the head of the wise man and is wisdom, so the wise man has the eyes of the intellect in wisdom.
comments.comment: Of the wise man, his eyes are in his head (Eccl 2:14). If 'Christ is the head of every man', and a man and the wise man are real, the head of the wise man is Christ; but our Christ is wisdom—'for wisdom was born to us from God' (1 Corinthians 1:30)—so the head of the wise man is therefore wisdom, in which the wise man has the eyes of the intellect, contemplating in it the words of things that have come to pass.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The eyes of the wise man are in his head in the sense that the head of a man is Christ, so the thinking faculty is in Christ.
comments.comment: Something strange is said in Ecclesiastes. To the one who does not understand it will seem senseless; but to the wise it has been said from Ecclesiastes: The eyes of the wise man are in his head. In what head? For of every human being, even of the senseless and the fool, the perceptible eyes are in a perceptible head; but the eyes of the wise man, the ones spoken of before, the ones lit by the Lord's commandment, are in his head — in Christ, since the head of a man is Christ, the apostle says. The thinking faculty is in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reason why the wise man's eyes are said to be in his head.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The head signifies the mind, so the wise have their eyes in it.
comments.comment: And often the head signifies the mind. … But also praiseworthily: 'The eyes of the wise are in his head' (Ecclesiastes 2:14). And he who, being not wise, has become wise, does not have them being carried around.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ends of the wise and the foolish may seem the same, but the wise man and the fool have nothing in common in how people remember them or in how God repays them.
comments.comment: Yet when I considered how the end of each of these two lives differs, I found no difference; and since I had made myself a companion of fools, I shall receive the wages of folly (Ecclesiastes 2:14-15). For what good is there in those clever arguments, or what profit in many words, when streams of idle talk pour out as from the spring of folly (Ecclesiastes 2:15)? Yet the wise man and the fool have nothing in common, neither in how people remember them nor in how God repays them (Ecclesiastes 2:16). Human affairs still seem to be beginning when their end already overtakes them all. But the wise man never shares the same end as the senseless.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: He came to hate a life spent on empty toil that someone else would inherit, and found the true goods to be the knowledge of wisdom and the gaining of courage.
comments.comment: So I came to hate my whole life, spent as it was on empty things, which I passed melting away over earthly toils (Ecclesiastes 2:17). For, in short, everything I labored over so painfully was the work of thoughtless impulse; and someone else will inherit it, whether wise or foolish, the cheerless fruit of my labors (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). But when I had set these things aside and thrown them away, the goods truly set before a human being came into view: the knowledge of wisdom and the gaining of courage (Ecclesiastes 2:20-21).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The 'choice of the spirit' is shown here to be a choice of the heart.
comments.comment: That it happens to a man in all his toil and in the choice of his heart, by which he toils under the sun (Eccl 2:22). From this it is shown that the choice of the spirit is a choice of the heart.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The man swept away by other things chooses evil, wickedness and toil, and is dragged about day and night by troubles of body and soul.
comments.comment: But if someone has not cared for these, and has been swept away by other things, such a man has chosen evil instead of good, pursued wickedness instead of kindness, and toil instead of rest (Ecclesiastes 2:22). He is dragged about by troubles of every kind, held in their grip night and day without end, by the pressing labors of the body and the ceaseless cares of the soul, while his heart writhes within him over strange things (Ecclesiastes 2:23).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The perfect good does not lie in eating and drinking, though food comes from God, and the good man receives heavenly joy from God while the wicked man is driven by greed.
comments.comment: For the perfect good does not rest in eating and drinking, even though food certainly comes to human beings from God (Ecclesiastes 2:24-25); for nothing given to us for our preservation lies outside His providence. But the good man, having received wisdom from God, has received heavenly joy; while the wicked man, driven by evils sent from God and sick with greed, is eager to heap up much, and hurries to cast reproach, before the Master of all, on the man whom God has honored, holding out useless gifts, having made deceitful and empty things the pursuits of his own wretched soul (Ecclesiastes 2:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the good in verses 24 to 26 is wisdom and heavenly joy, not food and drink.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Without Christ none can eat his flesh or drink his blood, symbols of virtue.
comments.comment: For who eats and who drinks besides him? (Eccl 2:25). For who without Christ will be able to eat his flesh or drink his blood, which are symbols of virtues and of knowledge (John 6:54)?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's eating and drinking as a figure of virtue and knowledge.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The sinner's gathering is likened to the proverb of wealth increased by interest, and it is the gathering of sins that he calls vanity.
comments.comment: And to the one sinning, he gave a distraction to add and to gather and to give the good before the face of God (Eccl 2:26); for even this is vanity and a choice of the spirit. This is like the proverb which says: 'He who increases his wealth with interest and abundance, to him who gives alms...' "He gathers the poor" (Proverbs 28:8) … However, it must be understood that he defined the gathering of sins as vanity, not that it was by chance for him to have a good teacher from God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Solomon divides the times of life's affairs, but the saving message reverses his words: there is a time to die and a time to be born.
comments.comment: The wise Solomon, dividing up the times of life's affairs and setting aside the right moment for each thing that happens, said: "There is a time for everything, and a season for every matter: a time to be born, and a time to die" (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2). But I would alter the wise man's saying just a little, and proclaim to you the saving message: there is a time to die, and a time to be born.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Human affairs swing between seeking and losing, killing and being killed, loving and hating, war and peace, quickly from what seemed good to evil.
comments.comment: Now someone has sought something, and now he has lost it; now he has kept it, and now he has let it go (Ecclesiastes 3:6); at one time he killed, at another he was killed; he spoke, then fell silent (Ecclesiastes 3:7); he loved, then hated (Ecclesiastes 3:8). For human affairs are now at war and now at peace (Ecclesiastes 3:8), as things swing quickly from what seemed good into what all admit is evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the point of the list of times: things in this life swing quickly between opposites.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: He would stop useless toils, since these things drive people to frenzy and a wicked watcher gapes over this age to destroy what God formed.
comments.comment: Let us stop, then, our useless toils (Ecclesiastes 3:9). For all these things, it seems to me, were set there to drive human beings into frenzy with venomous stings (Ecclesiastes 3:10). A wicked one who watches for his chance gapes greedily over this age, straining with all his might to destroy what God has formed, for he has chosen to make war on it from beginning to end (Ecclesiastes 3:11).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: God gave the senses and sensible things as a temporary distraction before purification, and after purification the pure one no longer sees them as only distracting but as holding meanings for spiritual contemplation.
comments.comment:
He saw, along with the distraction which God gave to the sons of men to be distracted in it, all things which He made beautiful in His time (Ecclesiastes 3:11), and He also gave eternity in their hearts, so that man might not find the work which God made from the beginning until the end (Ecclesiastes 3:11). …

He says, I saw the sensible things distracting the mind of man, which God gave before the purification to men so that they might be distracted in them. But he calls their beauty temporary and not eternal; for after purification, the pure one does not see sensible things as only distracting his mind, but as things dwelling within him for spiritual contemplation. For the mind is struck by the sensible through the senses, imposing itself sensorially, and in another way it prepares the meanings stored in the sensible things being seen; but this latter knowledge happens to the pure alone, while the comprehension of things through the senses happens to both the pure and the impure.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why God gave a 'distraction' and what the 'beautiful' things are.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Eternity in their hearts means the meanings of the age, the kingdom within us.
comments.comment: Therefore he also called the distraction temporary, given from God; for God, foreseeing the passionate soul, gave to it senses and sensible things, so that, being distracted and thinking through them, it might flee from those who are about to cast thoughts upon it from the opposing things. And He gave to them, he says, also eternity, that is, the meanings of the age; for this is the kingdom of heaven which the Lord said we should have within us (Luke 17:21), which, being covered by the passions, is not found by men. Therefore he says, he knew that the things themselves are not good, but the meanings of the things, upon which it is the nature of the rational to be glad and to do the good; for nothing feeds and gives drink to the mind like virtue and the knowledge of God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Things are beautiful in their time through timely use of God's gifts.
comments.comment: We make things good through the timely use of what God has given us; for in this way everything will be beautiful in its own time, and 'behold, all things are very beautiful' (Genesis 1:31).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The greatest goods are good cheer and doing good, and enjoyment comes from God only if righteousness guides one's actions, while eternal things cannot be added to or taken from.
comments.comment: I am convinced, then, that the greatest goods for a human being are good cheer and doing good (Ecclesiastes 3:12), and that even this passing enjoyment comes from God only if righteousness guides one's actions (Ecclesiastes 3:13). But from the eternal and incorruptible things that God has firmly fixed, nothing can be taken away and nothing added (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Yet to anyone at all, those things are at once fearful and wonderful. What has come to be stands fast, and what is still to be has already come to be, in that it is foreknown; and the one who suffers wrong has God for his helper (Ecclesiastes 3:15).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Since all things God has made shall be for ever, God did not make evil and evil shall not be for ever, and God made wisdom unchangeable so that lovers of knowledge might cease from evil.
comments.comment: He knew that all things which God has made shall be for ever; nothing can be added to them, and nothing can be taken from them, and God did this so that they might stand in awe of His face. If 'all things which God has made shall be for ever' (Eccl 3:14), then God did not make evil, and therefore evil shall not be for ever. … From the manifold wisdom nothing can be taken away, and to it nothing can be added. He made it, he says, so that men, being lovers of knowledge, might cease from evil; 'for all shall depart from evil by the fear of the Lord' (Proverbs 16:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why what God has made is permanent and what follows about evil.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: God seeks the one whom He enlightens with knowledge, and the persecuted are blessed because they shall know the contemplation of the things that have come to be.
comments.comment: That which has happened is already, and all things that are to happen have already happened, and God will seek the one who is being pursued. If 'blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 5:10), and the kingdom of heaven consists of the words of the ages of things happened and things to happen, then blessed are the persecuted, because they themselves shall know the contemplation of the things that have come to be. For this is what God is said to seek: the one whom He enlightens with knowledge, and not to seek the one whom He does not enlighten with knowledge. 'I wandered, says David, like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I have not attended to your commandments' (Psalm 119:176); and he himself was being persecuted: 'many, he says, are the ones driving me out and distressing me; from your testimonies I have not departed' (Psalm 119:157).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A pit receives the ungodly; another place, the godly.
comments.comment: I saw in the regions below a pit of punishment receiving the ungodly, and another place set apart for the godly (Ecclesiastes 3:16-17).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The life of man is called 'talk', since we must give an account of every idle word on the day of judgment.
comments.comment: There I said in my heart concerning the talk of the sons of men, that God judges them, and to show this that they are cattle (Eccl 3:18). He has now named the life of man as talk; for if we are to give accounts concerning every idle word on the day of judgment, in which both the pure and the impure are revealed.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Before God, he reasoned, righteous and unrighteous, reasoning and unreasoning creatures were alike, since all had the same breath and all returned to the same earth, and it was uncertain whether souls would fly upward.
comments.comment: And I reasoned that before God all things were regarded and judged alike: that the righteous and the unrighteous were the same, and so were creatures with reason and creatures without it (Ecclesiastes 3:18). For, I thought, a span of time was measured out to all alike, and death hung over them; before God the races of beasts and of human beings were the same, and they differed from one another only in articulate speech; everything befell them in much the same way, and death came no more to the other living creatures than to human beings (Ecclesiastes 3:19). All, I supposed, had the same breath, and human beings had nothing more (Ecclesiastes 3:19); in a word, all things were empty, taking their make-up from the same earth and bound to be dissolved into the same earth (Ecclesiastes 3:20). For it was uncertain, I thought, whether human souls would fly upward, and whether the other souls, those that beasts possess, would melt away downward (Ecclesiastes 3:21).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Life, death, sickness and wealth happen to the righteous and unrighteous alike, who are from the dust and return to it with one spirit, so the two cannot be told apart before the judgment.
comments.comment: He speaks of things commonly happening to all men, both the righteous and the unrighteous in this world, such as life, death, sickness, health, wealth, poverty, the loss of limbs, women, children, and possessions, from which it is not possible to distinguish the righteous from the impious before the judgment. He also says that it is common to them to be from the dust and to return again to the dust, and that they have one soul, not by number, but by nature; 'for spirit,' he says, 'is one for all' (Ecclesiastes 3:19). But now he has called the man who comes into honor and does not understand, but through irrational pleasures has been compared to the unthinking beasts and has become like them. But even through these things, the righteous and the unrighteous will not be clearly known before the judgment, because many unrighteous have turned to righteousness and been exalted, and many righteous have fallen from virtue and been humbled.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Preacher means by one fate for people and beasts and why the righteous cannot be told apart before the judgment.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Death did not belong to man as he was made but came from dishonor, and having fallen from the likeness of God in immortality he is made like the beasts in death.
comments.comment: The suffering of death, he says, was not attached to man as he was made, but came upon him from dishonor. For though he was honored with growth toward immortality, he did not perceive it, having a good from honor greater than his nature (Psalm 49:12). And so, having fallen away from the likeness of God that consists in immortality, he is made like the beasts in death. For as Ecclesiastes says: “As the death of this one, so the death of that one, and one spirit is in them all; and what advantage does man have over the beast? Nothing, for all is vanity. All things go to one place; all things came from the dust, and all things return to the dust” (Ecclesiastes 3:19-20).
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: Nothing is of more worth than spiritual joy in the works and virtues of man, and the one who falls from this joy will not return to do the things that bring it.
comments.comment: And I saw that there is nothing good except that which a man rejoices in regarding his works, because it is a part of him (Eccl 3:22); … So what excess did I find in these things? Now, nothing, he says. For all is vanity except for the spiritual joy, which is found to occur upon the works and the virtues of man; for the one who has fallen from this joy will not return again to do those things which contribute to its possession.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Slanders are the things set against us, and concerning the Savior Christ it is said that he will humble the slanderer.
comments.comment: And I turned back and saw with all the slanders that had happened under the sun; and behold, the tear of those being slandered, and there is no one to comfort them, and from the hand of those slandering them is strength, and there is no one to comfort them (Eccl 4:1). Slanders refers to those things set against us; … and again concerning the Savior Christ he says: 'and he will humble the slanderer and will stay with the sun.'
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The contest of slander is very great, and the crown laid up for it is greater still.
comments.comment: This contest of slander is not small but very great. So Solomon, wanting to present the harshness of the contest, says: "I saw the slanders that occur under the sun, and look—the tear of the slandered, and there was no one to comfort them" (Ecclesiastes 4:1). But if the contest is great, then, just as that is so, the crown laid up for it is greater still.
comments.author: Olympiodorus of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Seeing the oppressed with no one to comfort them, he judged that among the unjust the dead fare better than the living, and the one not yet born better than both, since he has not touched human wickedness.
comments.comment: Turning myself away from all these thoughts, I looked closely at all the kinds of oppression that roam among human beings, and I turned from them in disgust (Ecclesiastes 4:1). Through them some are wronged and weep and lament, struck down by force, while on every side there is no one at all to defend them or even to comfort them; and those who take the law into their own hands are lifted on high, from where they will also fall. Of the unjust and the reckless, those who have died have fared better than those who are still alive (Ecclesiastes 4:2). More to be preferred than both is the one who is to be like them but has not yet been born, because he has not yet touched the wickedness found among human beings (Ecclesiastes 4:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the dead and the unborn are called better.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: 'Better are the dead than the living' is said so that we may not fear death but desire it when the confession calls, leaving an example of dying well.
comments.comment: 'Better are the dead than the living,' (Ecclesiastes 4:2) says Qoheleth — that we may not fear death but desire it when the confession calls. Eleazar the aged scribe would not even pretend to eat swine's flesh: spitting it out, he went willingly to the rack, 'leaving the young a noble example, willingly and manfully to die a good death for the revered and holy laws.' (2 Maccabees 6:18–31) So we too, refusing base compliance, shall leave children and brethren an example worth more than life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the Preacher says the dead are better than the living.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man who explored every path of luxury and then counted the dead blessed above the living is a trustworthy accuser of luxury.
comments.comment: What then did this same man [Solomon] say after such abundance of wealth, possessions, luxury, and ease? “I counted the dead blessed above the living,” he said, “and better than both is the one who has not yet come into being” (Ecclesiastes 4:2). Truly this man is a trustworthy accuser of luxury, since he passes such a judgment on it. If someone who had lived in poverty and want had brought this verdict against luxury, he would seem to accuse it not from truth but from inexperience. But when the man who explored all of it and searched out every one of its paths dishonors it, the accusation is beyond suspicion.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: The Preacher praises those who have already died with Christ and are free from slanderers, and counts the one who was never born into malice as good.
comments.comment: … And I praised with the dead, those already dead, for the sake of the living, as many as they themselves live until now (Eccl 4:2); and a good one for these two, who has not yet become, who has not seen with the creation the evil thing made under the sun (Ecclesiastes 4:3). And I praised those already having died with Christ and having been released from those slandering them, for the sake of those living in malice and persisting in it until now. But he is good, neither being required of such a death separating him from malice, nor being born in malice, who did not know the evil toil being done by those slandering under the sun.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He sees all malice and the one acting manfully in it, and a zeal toward men that is vain, since God must become all in all and Christ be fulfilled.
comments.comment: And I saw with all the toil and with all the courage of the creation (Eccl 4:4), that it is the zeal of a man from his companion; and even this is vanity and a choice of the spirit. I saw, he says, all malice and the one acting manfully in it; for him also he says, acting manfully in impieties, slandering the poor, and again the creation as 'made to be played with by the angels' (Job 40:19) of God. I saw also all his zeal which he has toward men, being vain and making his heart confident; for it is necessary for God in all things to become all things and for Christ to be fulfilled, the prayer saying: 'Give them that they also may be in us one, just as we are one, Father' (John 17:21).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Envy from neighbors is the goad of an evil spirit and eats away the soul of the one who welcomes it, so a sensible person prefers one hand full of ease to two hands full of toil.
comments.comment: It also became clear to me how much envy pursues a man from his neighbors (Ecclesiastes 4:4), the goad of an evil spirit, and that the one who welcomes it and, as it were, clasps it to his breast is left with nothing but to eat away his own soul, to saw it through and wear it out along with his own body (Ecclesiastes 4:5), making the good fortune of others a grief past all comfort. A sensible person would rather fill one hand with ease and gentleness than both hands with toil and the cunning of a deceitful spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verses' envy, toil and 'one handful' in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Whoever does not work righteousness devours his flesh, infused with evils growing out of the flesh.
comments.comment: The fool took his hands and ate his flesh (Ecclesiastes 4:5). If the hands of practical work are a symbol, everyone not working righteousness takes his hands; therefore such a one, he says, devours his flesh, being infused with evils growing out of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the fool's 'eating his own flesh' as a figure for not working righteousness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A good fullness of rest is better than the fullness of two of toil, as a little with the righteous is better than much wealth of sinners, and it is better to learn one spiritual insight than many of foolish wisdom.
comments.comment:
A good fullness of a dragon of rest rather than the fullness of two dragons of toil and a choice of the spirit. The choice of the spirit seems to me to be a passionate psychological will; whence also the good dragon of virtue is preferred over the two dragons of malice and ignorance and the choice of the spirit. Such is also 'better is a little with the righteous than much wealth of sinners' (Psalm 37:16) and 'better is a little having with righteousness than many generations with injustice' (Psalm 37:16). Similar.

With these passages also come 'I would rather be cast out of the house of my God than dwell in the habitations of sinners' (Ps 4:7) and 'it is better to dwell on a corner of a roof than with a contentious woman in a shared house' (Ps 4:7), as someone said: it is better to learn one spiritual insight than a multitude of insights of foolish wisdom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The man with neither son nor brother has not received the spirit of adoption and starves his soul of the knowledge of God, though the words are also true of childless rich men.
comments.comment:
The man of Ps 4:8 is one and there is no second, and neither son nor brother is to him; and there is no end to all his toil, and indeed his eye is not filled by wealth (Ps 4:8). And for what do I toil and starve my soul from goodness? For this too is vanity and an evil distraction. If anyone does not have a brother, this one has not received the spirit of adoption, and if anyone is not a father, this one is evil; 'for he says, no offspring shall be born of the wicked' (Ecclesiastes 4:8). Appropriately, such a person is not filled by evil, starving his own soul from the knowledge of God.

But I say father and brother here according to the meaning of the Scripture; for I do not ignore that the propositions set forth are placed as if they were not true concerning sensible brothers and fathers. If anyone would also take the plain meaning of these sayings, he will be fully known as one of the childless rich and those striving to provide themselves a multitude of wealth, even if they were distant from friends; for these words spoken concerning men are entirely true.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Those who join their lives in partnership help each other up and double their good fortune, while the solitary man leads a grim existence and a threefold cord does not easily break.
comments.comment: Far better than he are those who have joined their lives in partnership, from which they may reap the best of fruits (Ecclesiastes 4:9). For when two men rightly devote themselves to the same affairs, even if some mishap befalls one of them, he still has no small help in the one who is with him; but for a man in trouble the greatest misfortune is to have no one to lift him up again (Ecclesiastes 4:10). Those who share a common life, on the other hand, double their good fortune and comfort each other through the winter of unwelcome events, so that by day they shine with the confidence they have in one another, and by night they are graced with gladness (Ecclesiastes 4:11). But the man who drags out a solitary life leads a grim existence for himself, never realizing that anyone who attacks men who stand close together makes a rash and unsafe plan, and that a threefold cord does not easily break (Ecclesiastes 4:12).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Without the Lord no one could be warmed, and the one being strengthened is the evil one, against whom stand the man and the angel of God so that the man becomes a third shoot not quickly broken.
comments.comment: And even if the two sleep, they are warm (Ecclesiastes 4:11); and how would one be warmed? Without the Lord, no one could become alive in the spirit; 'for the Lord is the spirit' (2 Cor 3:17). And if one is strengthened, the two will stand against him, and the third shoot will not quickly break through (Ecclesiastes 4:12). I think the one being strengthened is the evil one, against whom the two stand, both the man and the angel of God, so that the man, having conquered the devil, might be made worthy of the knowledge of God and become a third shoot not quickly being broken.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'two' and the 'third' in the verses as the man and the angel of God against the evil one.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A poor young man of sound mind is better than an old foolish king who forgot that a man can rise from prison and the king fall from his unjust power.
comments.comment: I prefer a poor young man of sound mind to an old and foolish king (Ecclesiastes 4:13), who never took it to heart that it is possible for someone from prison to be set up as king, and for himself to fall in the end, and justly, from his unjust power (Ecclesiastes 4:14). For it turns out that all those of the older generation who are placed under the young but sensible ruler live free from grief (Ecclesiastes 4:15). For those born afterward, having no experience of the other, cannot praise even this one, led as they are by thoughtless judgment and by the drive of a hostile spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:16).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: It is good to spare the tongue, for we speak within God's hearing and must not let slip whatever comes to mind, since dream images follow the soul's cares and idle chatter goes with folly.
comments.comment: It is good to spare the tongue, and to keep a steady heart in your eagerness to speak (Ecclesiastes 5:2). For we must not be careless about our words and let slip through the voice whatever comes into the mind, even when it is out of place. Rather, we must bear in mind that, though we stand far from heaven, we speak within God's hearing (Ecclesiastes 5:2), and that it pays to speak without stumbling. Just as all manner of dream images attend the varied cares of the soul, so idle chatter is yoked to folly (Ecclesiastes 5:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why speech must be careful: we speak within God's hearing.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Whatever you vow to God you must carry out at once, for delay is not without loss, and it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
comments.comment: For I say that we must remember him who speaks plainly through the most wise Moses: ‘You shall keep what goes out through your lips’ (Deuteronomy 23:23). That is, whatever you vow, hasten to carry it out, and very promptly. For in such matters delay is not without loss. ‘For if you make a vow to the Lord,’ it says, ‘do not delay in paying it’ (Deuteronomy 23:21; Ecclesiastes 5:4). ‘It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay’ (Ecclesiastes 5:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: To promise God something and then delay keeping it is a fault, and the servant who knew his duty and left it undone will be punished more than the one who did not know.
comments.comment:
Let us therefore see what it means to promise and to delay; for it is not always the large interval of time that the delay signifies, but the complete denial of the promise. For Jacob appears to have given to God the tenth parts after many years, while walking toward Mesopotamia, and Hannah bringing Samuel to God after a long time.

Regarding the gifts around the body, it is thus; but regarding the gifts of the soul and the body, how should one interpret delay? I think that he who promises correct faith and says it is a creation, delays one thing from the Holy Trinity; and he who promises to confess all things through God and introduces automatism again, delays; and regarding the other dogmas, likewise. Regarding virtues, it is thus: he who promises righteousness and is unrighteous, delays in fulfilling it; and he who promises temperance and is again committing fornication, delays. Regarding the things of the body: he who promises self-control and again takes on various bonds, delays; and he who promises virginity or monogamy and having married or having married a second time, delays in fulfilling it.

As for how 'it is good not to vow or to vow and not to fulfill,' we will solve this by bringing in the Gospel, that the servant who did not know and did not do will be punished little, but he who knew and did not do will be punished much. 'Do not give your mouth to sin your flesh, and do not say before the face of God that it is ignorance, so that God may not be angry at your voice and destroy the works of your hands' (Eccl 5:5-6). For in a multitude of dreams and vanities and many words—'In a multitude, he says, of dreams' (Eccl 5:7)—evil 'and of vanities and words' (Eccl 5:7) false, a man becomes, his works being destroyed from the abandonment of God, which happened to him because of his own lawlessness.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Flee a flood of fine-sounding words, for God hears them and the one who trusts them sees his works destroyed.
comments.comment: You must flee by every means the flood of such fine-sounding words, knowing that God will hear them (Ecclesiastes 5:6). For the one who sets his mind on such things gains nothing but to watch his own works being destroyed by God (Ecclesiastes 5:6). For as many dreams are empty, so too are many words (Ecclesiastes 5:7).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Do not wonder at oppression of the poor, but avoid seeming greater than the powerful, for wickedness will not rescue you.
comments.comment: So there is no need to wonder when you look at the poor being oppressed and at judges who reason dishonestly (Ecclesiastes 5:8). But you must avoid seeming to be greater than those who are more powerful (Ecclesiastes 5:8). For even if you should manage this, still wickedness, of itself, will not rescue you from the terrors that are to come upon you.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Do not be amazed at injustice among men as if there were no providence, for God preserves all things through Christ and provides for all through the holy angels.
comments.comment:
If you see oppression of the poor and the seizing of judgment and justice in a land, do not marvel at the matter; for high sits above high and the high ones are upon them (Eccl 5:8). And abundance of the land is upon everything, the work of the field of the king (Eccl 5:9). …

If you see, he says, among men some being slandered, others being treated unjustly in judgment, and others practicing righteousness, do not marvel at these things happening as if there were no providence. For know that God through Christ preserves all things, and this one again provides for all through the holy angels abounding in the knowledge of those on earth.
comments.selected_reason: Answers a common doubt, why injustice is allowed, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: God, the King of the world, will bring tribulation on those who prefer greed and give the knowledge of God and sweet rest to those who lived well, and the Lord has entrusted this world to angels.
comments.comment:
For God is the King of the world brought into being through him, who will give tribulation to those who prefer greed and the vanity of this life over the knowledge of Christ, but to those who have lived in goodness and have served in courage and righteousness, he will give the knowledge of God and sweet rest, even if they have known only a few things here or many words, knowing in part and prophesying in part; and the one will receive such an end, but the one filled with wickedness he will not allow the worm born of it to rest.

Since the Lord entrusted this world to angels, Moses shows by saying: 'When the Most High divided the nations, as he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of nations according to the number of the angels of God.' And the Lord our own in the Gospels named the world a field, saying: 'The world is a field.' And regarding the abundance of the earth, he says of those on earth, if indeed, 'Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth'; what other inheritance is there for rational nature besides the knowledge of God? And he called the angels high, because they partake of the high Lord: 'For high above all nations is the Lord,' he says.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A cultivated field shows that it has a king, as a driven chariot shows a charioteer and a rowed ship a pilot, even when he is not seen.
comments.comment: 'Abundance of the earth is in everything, a king of the cultivated field is there' (Ecclesiastes 5:9). In the literal sense: no one is lord, master, or ruler of a field while it is being blamed for bearing 'thorns and thistles' (Gen 3:18); but of a cultivated field, there is a king. He calls the king the owner. In the literal sense: if you see a cultivated field, know that it has a master and a king; just as if you see a chariot being driven in the manner of a charioteer, you realize you are receiving the impression of a charioteer; and if you see a ship being rowed and it must be steered in a certain way, you receive the impression of a pilot, even if you do not see him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the verse speaks of a king of the field.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A field in order points to its ruler, as a fabric points to a weaver, and a soul well farmed and sown in tears likewise has a king.
comments.comment: And those who occasionally introduce the idea that God's providence rules all things, say, if they are constructing something, that it is providence; just as a fabric clearly shows that there is a weaver, even if the weaver does not appear, so one, seeing a cultivated field, receives the impression that it has a leader and a ruler. … But it is also more powerful and more public to say so, if one sees a soul like a cultivated field, having been tilled, in bloom, with produce and trees and a multitude of produce. For 'one bore a hundred, another sixty, another thirty' (Matthew 13:8). When you see, therefore, a soul thus being farmed and having 'sown in tears' (Ps 126:5) and having itself ready for 'reaping in joy' (Ps 126:6), of this cultivated thing there is a king, a word meaning a leader, a word meaning one ruling and reigning.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Church, with its right teaching and good works, is a field whose king is the practical life, but where there are false teachers the field has a tyrant or a robber.
comments.comment: But one should also take another analogy: the Church of God, according to the pious doctrines and the ethical works, and those who practice them, are called a field. … The practical life is a king for this field, because it has worked. But when you see false teachers and "churches committing adultery", know that this field has not worked truly; it does not have a king who praises it, but rather a tyrant or a robber. For robbers and tyrants especially pursue the wilderness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who loves material things is never filled, but the one who loves the words of the Lord will be filled with refined silver, so the verse speaks of fake silver.
comments.comment: "He who loves silver will not be filled with silver" (Eccl 5:10). As for the literal sense: the one desiring material things is never filled, … It can be said concerning silver here: "it is not praised". For the one loving "the words of the Lord" will also be filled with "refined silver". For he does not always know "in part", nor, having transitioned from "out of the fullness", does he remain in the "from the fullness", but he will encounter eventually to approach "face to face" (1 Cor 13:12) the truth and to acquire the very "fullness" of the mind of Christ. … Therefore, the discourse is concerning fake silver.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Greed is never satisfied: what is added to wealth only kindles the appetite for more, and the greedy person, as Hades never does, never says 'Enough'.
comments.comment: You are eager to add ten more talents to your ten; when they become twenty, you seek another twenty, and what is added never stops your impulse but kindles your appetite. … Whatever the eye sees, the greedy person desires. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the money-lover with taking (Ecclesiastes 5:10 [4:8 LXX]). Hades never said, “Enough,” and the greedy person never said, “Enough.” … When will you use what you have? When will you enjoy it, always gripped by the labors of acquisition?
comments.selected_reason: Shows in everyday terms why the lover of silver is never satisfied.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The man who craves money never has his fill, hoarding wealth brings sleepless nights, and the wealth must perish while he himself departs as he came.
comments.comment: Just as a possession seized by robbery is most harmful and most unholy, so the man who craves money never has his fill, nor does he win the goodwill of his neighbors, even if such men gain ever so vast a sum of silver (Ecclesiastes 5:10). For this is vain. But goodness gladdens beyond measure those who keep company with it and makes them strong, granting them the power to see each thing clearly (Ecclesiastes 5:11). It is a great thing, too, not to cling to such cares. The poor man, even if he is a slave and has not stuffed his belly full, enjoys the gentle rest that sleep brings; but the desire for wealth lives with sleepless nights and weariness of soul (Ecclesiastes 5:12). What could be more absurd than to hoard up wealth with great effort and care and keep it safe, guarding for oneself the source of countless evils (Ecclesiastes 5:13)? That wealth must one day perish and be destroyed, whether its owner has children or not (Ecclesiastes 5:14). And he himself, even if he does not wish it, must fall to the earth and depart just as he was when he first came into being (Ecclesiastes 5:15).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The slave who obeys from fear of judgment and abstains from evil sleeps sweetly, but he has the spirit of slavery and is not yet a son.
comments.comment: He says that in time, in a certain way, he is a slave, obedient and private in his knowledge—and he is rich, having gathered many observations—and the sleep of one who thinks himself a slave and a slave-servant is sweet, whether he perceives little or much. And if he has the practice, so that this slave may have the 'spirit' of 'slavery,' he is not yet a 'son.' He is subject to the fear of judgment and 'abstains' from evil—if it must be said that he abstains—from the 'fear of punishment.' This, then, is a slave moved by the fear of the law.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wealth can hold its owner instead of the owner holding it, so that the lover of silver becomes a slave to mammon and endures all pains for his gain.
comments.comment: Another, thinking to be in many things, but having erred, has the care that does not permit him to sleep, a vain care. There is a sickness, which I saw under the sun (Ecclesiastes 5:13), a wealth guarded by one for his own wickedness, and that wealth will be lost in evil distraction. He says such things: For what is the purpose of someone's wealth? It is evident that even there the master of wealth is the wealth itself. This, then, is the one who has a sweetness from someone, and he himself is the master of the wealth; just as he is able to use the wealth well, holding it and not serving it, that is, the mammon (Matt 6:24), in this way wealth can hold the possessor; and woe to him, when he becomes a lover of silver, when he becomes a slave to mammon. He says, therefore, that such is 'wealth guarded by it.' He did not say simply the wealth itself, but 'guarded by it.' This is the wealth of the possessor. Thus also: how all painful things are endured for the sake of his acquisition.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sickness is wealth guarded for itself, which shows great wickedness and leaves its keeper without the wisdom of God.
comments.comment: There is a sickness which I saw under the sun, wealth being guarded by it for its own wickedness. The abundance of wickedness is now shown by wealth; and this wickedness is signified by sickness. … Therefore, everyone guarding this wealth for himself will not know the wisdom of God, nor will he cast his heart into understanding
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Providing for children is only a fine-looking excuse for greed, and wealth gathered with labor may prepare material of sins for others, so the soul should be given its inheritance first.
comments.comment: “But wealth is necessary because of the children.” This is a fine-looking excuse for greed. For you put forward the children, but you fill up your own heart. Do not blame the blameless one. The child has his own master, his own steward. From another he received his life, from him he awaits the resources of life. Were the Gospels not written for those who have married? “If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions, and give to the poor” (Matthew 19:21). When you asked the Lord for children, when you thought it right to become a father of children, did you add this: “Give me children, so that I may disobey your commandments? Give me children, so that I may not reach the kingdom of heaven?” And who will be the guarantor of the child’s choice, that he will use what is given to him as he ought? For to many people wealth has become a servant of licentiousness. Or do you not hear Ecclesiastes saying: “I saw a grievous sickness, wealth kept by its owner to his own harm” (Ecclesiastes 5:13)? And again: “I am leaving it to the man who comes after me” (Ecclesiastes 2:18). “And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool?” (Ecclesiastes 2:19). See to it, then, that after gathering wealth with countless labors, you do not prepare material of sins for others, and then be found punished doubly: for the wrongs you yourself committed, and for the wrongs you supplied to another.
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse's sickness of hoarded wealth to the excuse of providing for children.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The sickness is that neither the owner nor his heirs enjoy the wealth, for it is lost in distraction, as with the man who buys slaves who die, builds ships that are wrecked, and sows and loses even the seed.
comments.comment:
And the terror of the sickness is this: neither he himself enjoys it, nor does any of his successors. Furthermore, is it not 'that wealth will be lost in evil distraction'? There is wealth being lost by suddenness or by being snatched away by wars or robbers having become strong and finding and taking it. … This is not being taken in distraction. But when someone becomes a sailor or does other things for the sake of mobile wealth to gain much, often he is lost in the distraction. …

There was a time when we had in our hands: “God has given the sons of men an evil distraction” (Eccl 1:13). Often he buys slaves and they die; he builds ships and they are wrecked; he sows and loses even the seed. So in distraction it is lost — not in profligacy, not in idleness of hands. “And he begot a son, and there is nothing in his hand” (Ecclesiastes 5:14). “Just as he came out naked from his mother’s womb, he will return to go as he came” (Eccl 5:14). Men make children their excuse when they gather wealth; indeed they sometimes do wrong and plunder and do other things, saying, “I do this for the children’s sake.”
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A son may leave as he came, without what his father valued, since many who loved the learning of this world had sons who did not.
comments.comment: Many who possessed the things of “falsely-named knowledge” (1 Tim 6:20) or of Greek philosophy did not have sons who were lovers of these things; rather their sons depart together with them, having acquired nothing in the same way. Many unlearned men, at any rate, have become sons of wise men. This son, then, departs as he came: he came without such instruction and departs without it. But this too is possible: that one begets him who is reputed wise in this way — begets someone in wickedness, in licentiousness, the other kinds of evil — and he comes out naked of what the father was zealous for. The father was zealous, though, not at all about the kinds of evil, but about glory and “falsely-named knowledge.”
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man zealous for wealth gains nothing from it, neither enjoying it nor ruling his son, and at death returns as poor as he was born, able to take only the soul's goods.
comments.comment: I saw, then, one zealous for wealth, and the wealth profited him nothing: for he neither enjoyed it, nor became master of the son he had, but is altogether poor, just as he was when born — born without money, without clothing. Again, “in the hand of the son” means “in the son’s power there is nothing.” We are accustomed to say, “he has the wealth under his hand.” When, then, the day of death comes, he returns again without dignity, without authority, taking nothing from this life; only the soul’s goods can one take up.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The evil is ignorance, and as the man came into the world with it, with it he will leave, whereas Job, a righteous man, goes naked free from malice and wickedness.
comments.comment:
An evil distraction is ignorance which, through punishment, separates the unclean from spiritual contemplation. Just as he went out from his mother's womb naked (Ecclesiastes 5:15), he will return to go his way as he has come, and he will take nothing from his labor, so that he may go with nothing in his hand (Eccl 5:15). And this too is an evil sickness; for just as it came to be, so it will depart.

And Job says: 'Naked I came out from the womb of my mother, and naked I will depart there' (Job 1:21); but the one here says 'just as he went out from his mother's womb naked, he will return to go his way as he has come' (Ecclesiastes 5:15). But Job, as a righteous man, goes naked, free from malice and wickedness; but this one, with that ignorance by which he came into this world, with this also he will depart there.
comments.selected_reason: Compares the man with Job to show what the verse means.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wisdom and habits are called mothers, as people are called sons of perdition or of light, and this man's mother, wickedness, brought him forth, so he enters having acquired nothing.
comments.comment: I say that wisdom is the mother of the wise man: “for wisdom was justified by her children” (Matt 11:19); and the children of wisdom are the wise. “And your mother will guide you” — wisdom. And again, habits — the worse and the better — are called mothers of the things done according to them. So too one is called “son of perdition” (John 17:12), “son of vipers” (Matt 3:7), “of death,” “son of light” (Luke 16:8), and another “son of peace” (Luke 10:6). Here we take the blameworthy mother, since the person under discussion is not an excellent one. According to the anagogy he has a blameworthy mother: just as his mother — wickedness — brought him forth, so he enters here having acquired nothing, in opposition to what his father — who gathered toilsome wealth — provided, and his mother, the habit that bore him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He will leave taking nothing of his toil, and he stores up not knowing for whom he gathers.
comments.comment: He will turn back to go as he has come, and he will take nothing of his toil. The fact of the history is clear: he takes nothing of what he labored for. He lets them go and did not know at the time, even if they come upon his enemies. 'He stores up,' he says, 'and does not know for whom he gathers them' (Psalm 39:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The verse can mean that he takes nothing, though if taken as a partial denial he takes with him the good he does with his money and office, and what he gathers for the wind does not remain.
comments.comment: But concerning sensible and human things it is said: “Do not fear when a man grows rich and the glory of his house is multiplied, for when he dies he will not take all things” (Psalm 49:16-17). Here the pretext that says “he will not take all things” is not a partial denial but a universal one — instead of “nothing.” And if you wish to take it literally as a partial privative denial, it says this: that there are things one does take — if, having money, he does good; if, having glory and office, he reaches out to the helpless and tries to help — from his zealous labors he takes these with him: … If, then, “in his abundance he toils for the wind” (Ecclesiastes 5:16), what he gathers does not remain.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man's toil becomes wind because his wealth is not his own, and his days are darkness, meaning ignorance, and mourning, so that he has died while living.
comments.comment: And what is his abundance, for which he toils toward the wind? His toil becomes wind, that is, his wealth is being overturned by nature; it is not becoming his own, not being held, so as even to be sent to a son. And indeed all his days are in darkness and in mourning. Darkness here means ignorance and the lack of clarity of things. And he mourns, missing those things which he hoped for, from which he thinks he has a pleasant life. And something stands before him. For mourning is raised up over death. In a certain way, therefore, he has died while living, 'and all his days are in darkness and he mourns' (Ecclesiastes 5:17). 'And the one who squanders,' he says, 'has died while living' (1 Tim 5:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One about to depart with empty hands toils for nothing, serving the wind, after a life of unholy desires and griefs, so that his days are darkness and his life mourning.
comments.comment: As he is about to depart with empty hands, he adds to his own wickedness, as if he did not consider that an end of life like his birth lies before him, and that he toils for nothing, serving some gust of wind rather than his own purpose (Ecclesiastes 5:16), after spending his whole life in most unholy desires and senseless impulses, and in griefs and sicknesses besides (Ecclesiastes 5:17). In short, for such a man the days are darkness and life is mourning.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Eating and drinking and enjoying one's labor are God's gift, and the knowledge of God is named by the intellect food, drink, goodness, portion, wealth, joy and gift.
comments.comment:
Behold, what I saw was good, which is beautiful: to eat and to drink and to see goodness in all his labor (Ecclesiastes 5:18), by which he labors under the sun, a number of the days of his life which God gave to him (Eccl 5:18); for it is a portion of Him. And indeed every man to whom God gave wealth and possessions, and empowered him to eat from it and to take his portion and to be joyful in his labor (Eccl 5:18), this is a gift of God (Eccl 5:19). For he will not remember many of the days of his life; for God distracts him with the joy of his heart.

The knowledge of God is called by the intellect food and drink and goodness and portion and wealth and possessions and joy and distraction of God and light and life and gift; and the Holy Spirit sets many other names upon knowledge, which it is not possible now to recount, unless the rule of the scholia permits.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A saying such as 'Let us eat and drink' must be read according to the speaker, for the same writer speaks there in the person of those who say there is no life after this one.
comments.comment:
One must take the words toward those speaking. If the speaker is wise, one must listen to them wisely. If, being wise, he personifies another face and brings it appropriately to that man, one must again listen to the conversation in that person. Since the apostle himself says: 'whether we eat or whether we drink, we neither lack nor exceed' (1 Corinthians 8:8), whether we are Christians or wise.

Or 'slaves of Christ', we have neither addition nor subtraction from the eating of anything still. But when he says, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (1 Corinthians 15:32), it is the same scribe, the same one speaking, but not from his own person, not as an apostle speaks, but he took the persona of those saying that beyond this present life, there is no life after these things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Enjoying one's labors with gladness, over possessions given by God and not seized by robbery, is a gift of God.
comments.comment: Yet this is good and not to be cast aside, for it is a gift of God: that a person can enjoy his own labors with gladness, having received possessions given by God and not seized by robbery (Ecclesiastes 5:18-19). For such a man is not sick with griefs, nor is he much enslaved to evil thoughts; he measures out his life in good deeds toward all, glad of heart and rejoicing in the gift of God (Ecclesiastes 5:20).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the enjoyment as God's gift when the goods were given by God and not seized by robbery.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Judas received spiritual wealth but was not empowered by it, having given away the truth for gain.
comments.comment: To contrast those who indeed received wealth of wisdom and knowledge, but did not indeed preserve it, it is said, 'and empowered him' (Ecclesiastes 5:19). For even the traitor Judas received intellectual wealth and spiritual possessions, but he was not empowered by them, having given away wisdom and the truth of God for the sake of gain.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The power to eat, take a share and be glad in one's labor is itself a gift of God, though some fail to use it through stinginess or sickness.
comments.comment: The power to eat from it, to take a part of it, and to be glad in its labor—this is a gift of God. Wealth was given to a man so that he might eat and be glad from it, and therefore this gift was from God. … Often one uses the gift and enjoys what is in it, but sometimes one fails to do so, either because he himself, through much stinginess, consumes nothing toward being glad, or because he is hindered by sickness or some other circumstance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly what is the gift of God in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not everything God gives is a spiritual gift: wealth, health, life and the authority of rulers are gifts of God but sensible and human, unlike a word of wisdom or knowledge.
comments.comment:
I was saying what even the apostle says: 'that I often intended to come to you' (Romans 1:13). For what reason then? 'That I might impart to you a spiritual gift' (Romans 1:11). And I was saying that not all things given by God are spiritual gifts. Whenever anyone receives a 'word of wisdom,' a 'word of knowledge,' and some other virtue, he has received a spiritual grace; but not if someone receives wealth or health or something of that kind; he has received a gift of God and a grace, but not a spiritual one.

The Lord 'causes death and makes alive' (1 Sam 2:6). If He 'makes alive,' meaning grain, wine, this very life, He has provided, but not a spiritual gift. The Lord 'appoints kings and removes them' (Dan 2:21). The authorities given to the rulers are certainly not 'spiritual gifts.' And the grace here, which is the gift, is not spiritual, being sensible and human.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man with much money can eat and drink only what suffices, and that is God's gift, while one who goes beyond what is necessary has gifts of pleasure instead.
comments.comment: If he has much money, if he has myriads of grain and much wine, he is not able to eat or drink everything, but he has a gift; which he is able to receive, the sufficient food, even until being satisfied, and that similarly, 'this is a gift of God.' If, therefore, anyone eats or drinks beyond what is necessary, he does not have these things as a gift of God, but as gifts of pleasure.
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse to ordinary eating and drinking.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives wisdom as wealth, that a man may eat the bread of wisdom.
comments.comment: And toward the ascent, thus: God gives wisdom and the 'wealth' in wisdom. And the 'existing things,' the contemplations of wisdom, so that the man might eat and drink from which he received, the bread of wisdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A portion of the gift is given to each according to his power, as a trainer gives athletes different amounts of food and the master in the parable of the talents gave each according to his ability.
comments.comment: If, for example, a trainer provides food to athletes and to those around the contest—for he also has others like bodyguards—he gives to each according to a proportion: to one athlete seven pounds of meat—and this is his portion—to another four; and to the one not competing, he gives two. Thus, a portion is given to each according to his power and his capacity. In this way also the parable of the talents in the Gospel occurred. He gave to each of his slaves his own silver, 'to each according to his own ability, to the one five, to the other two, and to the other one' (Matthew 25:15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spiritual nourishment, like the water Jesus gives, remains with a man and is not a brief refreshment, and the one who opens the inner eyes will be filled with bread.
comments.comment:
Since a more human expression is sometimes used, you know that there are things called sensible comforts for prayers, not only for eating, but also for removing sorrows; and these, therefore, are the spiritual nourishments. And someone receives in order to be glad, and receives a 'portion' so that it may remain with him. He is not only gladdened and fed and drinks from a brief encounter, but also continuously. For he continues drinking from the spring and the water which Jesus gives, and it remains with him. For he has within himself a spring having become a source for eternal life.

And again: 'Open your eyes and be filled with bread' (Proverbs 20:13). The one who opens the eyes of the 'inner man' 'shall be filled with bread'. And the loaves, therefore, thus remain like 'the spring which changes into eternal life'. And this has become useful by way of history, when the widow in Sarepta of Sidon, having only a few drachmae, fed Elijah and she herself had nothing, until prosperity came from the rain (1 Kings 17:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: True knowledge is a distraction from God, separating the purified soul from sensible things.
comments.comment: Regarding spiritual knowledge, few remember this kind of life and the sensory life, since his heart is always occupied with contemplation. A true knowledge, which separates the purified soul from sensible things, is a distraction from God.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The man who does not remember many things has hope only for the present, and God distracts him in these things so that the soul does not become motionless.
comments.comment: Something greater happens. He does not remember many things, but has hope only for the present, saying, 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). Therefore, is this what it means that 'God distracts him' (Ecclesiastes 5:20)? He distracts him in these things, since he does not want to acquire the preceding things, nor does he labor for the taking up of them. So that the soul does not become motionless, other things are given to it. And I said this at the beginning of the book, when I had it: 'God gave a wicked distraction.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To live by philosophy and virtue is the true life, but men attend to pleasant distractions and so do not remember the divine life of reason and contemplation, as distinct from the common life shared with animals.
comments.comment:
Therefore, the ascent: 'that he does not remember many of the days of his life, because God distracts him in the joy of his heart' (Ecclesiastes 5:20). To live according to philosophy and virtue is the chief and true life. And men do not remember many things, nor do they do much regarding that; they attend only to those who distract them and bring pleasant things, and they strive only about those things which they collect. But it was necessary to remember many things of those which will be useful to his life truly.

And here, then, is the common life, according to which we feel, according to which we have the soul yoked to the body, and according to which irrational animals move and perceive. The divine life, according to reason and contemplation, is the particular life of this man. Therefore, does he not remember this? He does not remember those things contributing to this life, if he has something futile.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The heart in this verse is the mind that sees God, though in the literal sense the man rejoices in a heart he wanted to feed on pleasure.
comments.comment: Again, here 'heart' for us is the true mind, which sees God. For instance, the saint says 'with boldness' to God: 'my heart was not stuck to me through scandal' … Again, others have 'fleshly hearts, in which the Spirit of the living God writes.' And he says 'fleshly' meaning those receptive to the writing of the Spirit. It is also possible, according to the literal sense, that he rejoices in his own heart. For he desired to have a heart feeding on pleasure.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The evil is common among men, but the wise man who has wealth or glory uses it differently from the many.
comments.comment: It is an evil that I saw under the sun (Ecclesiastes 6:1), and it is much among men; a man, to whom God will give wealth and substance and glory. These are held by evils; and this evil I 'saw under the sun' (Eccl 1:9) and especially it abounds among men. … The wise man, if he has 'wealth', uses the wealth differently than the many-man; the one having 'glory' does not think greatly upon the glory, but also adorns it along with himself.
