Joseph once had glory, and his own virtue adorned it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the wise man differs in his use of wealth and glory.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The chapter is about those worthy of knowledge who fell, and a long-lived man ignorant of God.
comments.comment: In this chapter he speaks about those deemed worthy of dispassion and knowledge who again fell through the envy of the devil. The second chapter contains the life of an unclean and much-toiling man, long-lived and not having known God, for whom the abortion is preferred to be, and for him after death a place of the same.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Wealth, poverty and glory are in themselves neither good nor evil, and the man who looks to the unseen things is neither lifted up by wealth nor sunk by poverty.
comments.comment:
And in shipwrecks, one bears neither poverty well, nor wealth, nor glory; from which it is evident that these things, by the very word, are indifferent. For if anyone is able to use them well and for good, by the very word they are neither good nor evil. They are able to have a good use and a useful use, a graspable and praiseworthy one. … Thus, the one who has ascended above human life and is able to say, 'I look not at the visible things, but at the invisible things' (2 Cor 4:18), knows that the visible things are temporary, but the invisible are eternal; he is not weakened by them, nor does wealth lift him up, nor does poverty sink him, nor does he seem to have acquired a great evil from a lack of glory. And from the honor and fame of the many, he does not consider himself to have anything.

But what of the ascent? They are rich and glorified in the 'wisdom of this age and of the rulers of this age that are passing away' (1 Cor 2:6). These do not rightly use either glory or prudence. And because of this, they are examined in great sin. For the wise man, even if he lacks one of these, conducting himself magnanimously, is not under evil; he is not at all sick but is healthy, and according to virtue he is healthy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man may obtain all he desires and still be unable to enjoy it, because sickness, misfortune or robbers deprive him of it.
comments.comment:
To those thinking highly of themselves, believing they are wise and seeming to be prudent, and that they are not 'mastered by these things' (Ecclesiastes 6:2); sometimes they obtain what they desire. And it seems to them that 'nothing of theirs is lacking to the soul' (Ecclesiastes 6:2), thinking they have acquired all 'wealth' of the soul and all 'glory', yet they do not have the power to use them.

Take for me someone who has grasped a great position, but has fallen into misfortune, such that he is no longer progressing; the power of the position is of no use to him. And indeed, we have known such people many times. … Thus the rich man, remembered with Lazarus (Luke 16:19), had everything, and 'possessions and wealth and glory' (Luke 16:19). And he received 'to master' them there, but after this, a deprivation of them occurred, and also of the pleasure upon them; and the one who heard: 'Fool, this very night they demand your soul from you (Luke 12:20). But what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?'

Others, having these things abundantly and very richly, are not permitted to be filled by them; they are prevented from having enjoyment, either through sickness or through some other circumstance. Because a stranger man eats him; and indeed this is also futility and sickness. … And this happens in many ways; sometimes he falls to robbers and his wealth is taken from him. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how a man can have wealth and still not enjoy it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The vanity is that a man who laboured for his possessions cannot keep them or enjoy them, and others enjoy what he worked for.
comments.comment:
It is taken away, and his own things go to others and are overpowered by someone, and another enjoys those things which he himself worked for. By way of comparison: many have often used things which others have written about with words, not being of their own opinion or glory. Often indeed wise men find books, into which others have labored, and both they and others are nourished by them and are glorified, when they are able to overturn them.

"And this too is vanity" (Ecclesiastes 6:2). Vanity is the not-retaining and not-enjoying of one's own.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The stranger who eats the wealth is the one who destroys the wealth of knowledge and wisdom, and 'eating' can mean destruction.
comments.comment: He who destroys the wealth enriched in all knowledge and all wisdom is evil, whom he also calls stranger and alien regarding the knowledge of God. The 'eating' is also said regarding food and regarding destruction: 'If you wish and listen to me, he says, eat the good things of the earth; but if you do not wish and do not listen to me, a sword shall strike you'—instead of 'destroys'. For the mouth of the Lord spoke these things. And this stranger, having also come to David, was persuaded to sacrifice the lamb of the poor; for Nathan the prophet called him a stranger then.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Begetting a hundred children or living many years gains a man nothing, since even many children do not prevent deaths.
comments.comment: If a man should beget a hundred, and live many years and a multitude, because his days shall be many. He has said the external pursuits for men: "wealth, possessions, glory". … No one at all begets a hundred. Let us say, even if someone is able to beget a hundred from various women; even this provides him no more. For kings indeed become fathers of many children, and this will not prevent deaths. For if he does not have one child, he certainly fails; and he does not have more than this, and even if he has a thousand; for they are not certainly saved in the wars. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Long life and bodily goods do not last, and even those begotten by a man's teaching can be taken from him.
comments.comment:
Appropriately he has said such things, "wealth, possessions, glory" and the others. And he says the bodily goods. Even if someone is not born in sorrows and lives many years, since his life has remained a long time, it is vain, having the promise only until the present life. Because of this, he strives in vain.

But what about the comparison? If someone through instruction begets many and strives to have a long-lasting glory in life, he does not become unchangeable. It is possible to be taken away from the children; for example, this Arius who among us begot many according to teaching and imitation of life. For indeed all were almost by him, and they were turned away, and all left him, and he did not have other men hating him as those begotten by him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many days of life are of no benefit by themselves, since in a multitude of days more sins are found.
comments.comment:
A multitude shall be his days of years. This he says: "he lived a thousand years of days". A multitude of days has become his. But the many-dayed life will benefit him nothing, since thus he receives it according to this time measured by the sun.

Another becomes long-lived upon the good earth, and the multitude of days benefits him. Indeed, it is said in the manner of a promise: 'I will fill him with length of days.' If it is 'better to depart and be with Christ,' then he who remains in the body laments much time, saying, 'Woe, that my sojourning has been lengthened' (Psalm 120:5); how then is the long-liver and the multitude of days given in the manner of a blessing? This is what it means: whatever years a man may live in this life, they are written down; and the multitude of days will not benefit him at all. For sometimes in the multitude of his days, more sins of his are found and many transgressions.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a long life is not in itself a blessing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The days that truly count are those lit by the sun of righteousness, and the blessed life of virtue is greater than many earthly years because it is eternal.
comments.comment: But he, having those days increasing, preparing the sunrises of the sun of righteousness, as was said a little before, possesses an enjoyment of the things above that exceeds being under the sensible sun. To whatever extent one has approached virtue, he has been enlightened by it. And the days become many in proportion to how much virtue holds sway. … That is to say: from life with virtue, one becomes long-lived, long-lasting, and blessed. If he tests these days in virtue, he will not desire to remain for other years. If the vain life should turn away from life, since he has hope in God, he becomes victorious over all of them, and it is vain for him to live many years. For many years are written down, but the blessed life is greater; it is eternal.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is better not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and despised it, as with one for whom it would have been good not to have been born.
comments.comment:
Peter alludes in the second epistle: 'it was better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, or to have known and to have turned back from the holy commandment handed down to them' (2 Pet 2:21). For he does not say at all that it is good to not have known the way of righteousness, but rather it is better not to have known than to have known and to despise it.

He has not said other things as regarding Judas, just as the Savior said: 'it was good for him, if he had not been born' (Matt 26:24). It was good for him, if he had not been called; if he had not been called, he would not have betrayed. It would not have been otherwise good for Saul, if he had not been king; for he did not fall among the lawless, among whom he fell after becoming king.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense the unborn is said to be better, by a comparison with Peter and the Savior's words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man who has wealth, possessions and glory always wants more, and the longer life he gains does not fill his soul.
comments.comment:
But another life does not receive this temporal life; I say this to those who think it is only this. For they said, 'hoping in this life alone', 'let us eat and drink' (1 Corinthians 15:32). And even if something is received in this way, it is not the long-lasting life. They go 'to the lake of fire' (Matt 25:41) and 'have a great penalty of fire' (Matt 25:46), where they have become part of the lot of death, clearly giving judgments against this life. And his soul will not be filled with goodness, and even a burial did not happen to him.

As it has happened, he says, 'wealth and possessions and glory'; he is not immersed in these. Just as he who loves wants to have even more silver and other things, so also he who wants to live luxuriously. For he does not yet want to encounter death. And his ascent is this: whoever is glorified as wise having 'falsely named' 'knowledge', still wants to be more greatly glorified. If he lives according to 'falsely named knowledge', he wished to always have it thus. And even a burial did not happen to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man may live a thousand years full of pleasant things and still be cast out unburied, and the stillborn, which never had any of them, is better than he.
comments.comment: He says that 'he lived many years of descent'. A thousand years happened, filled with all things pleasant, he misses nothing; and often without burial he is cast away. 'Better the corpse than this', in which nothing pleasant existed; nor did the shroud have wealth, nor possessions, nor was he glorified, and it is better than this, because he has not experienced any of these at all. This is applied to the literal sense. … Toward the upward leading, then, it is this: he strove much and grew rich, as if living in vanity with a false opinion, not knowing with clarity, being filled up, 'and there was no burial for him.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hundred children and thousand years are said by way of hyperbole, which exaggerates the truth for emphasis without lying, as the apostle also speaks.
comments.comment:
Again, they say in this way 'descents' are cycles of years. Each year has a certain beginning, which we call his 'descent'. … But how is it according to the explicit text and improbable and impossible? It is not improbable nor impossible; it has been spoken in a hyperbolic manner. And things spoken by way of hyperbole are not improbable and impossible—impossible at times, but not improbable. For someone will say thus: if a man is able to beget ten, he is able to beget a hundred, and to live so many years, if he lived fifty. The former, Methuselah, lived near a thousand. Therefore, the word is a hyperbole for the sake of emphasis, exaggerating the truth.

When the height of the cities constructed by those before Israel who possessed the land is spoken of, saying, 'we saw cities there with walls, whose walls reached even to the heaven', it was spoken hyperbolically. And the apostle also knew the logic of hyperbole and the use of the name. 'And still, by way of hyperbole, I say to you: if I have all knowledge and know all the mysteries, but do not have love, I benefit nothing' (1 Cor 13:2). For it is not profitable to know knowledge and all the mysteries without divine love. 'If we have all the faith so as to remove mountains, not having love, the greatness of the faith is nothing' (Matt 17:20). He says love is greater and that it is faith; and he gives it the power to say the mountains are removed; this is not lying, even if it exaggerates.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The miscarriage is said to be better off than the man who grew rich and whose abundance leaves nothing behind.
comments.comment:
The miscarriage spoke something good for him, that he came in vanity and walks in darkness (Ecclesiastes 6:4). According to the spoken word concerning the one who grew rich in all possessions, of whom nothing of the abundance remains—not moving, not still, not a glory, not a dignity—and if, having died, he is found outside all these, 'it is a good thing the miscarriage for this one,' which is the one who has not been fully tested by this life.

And toward such an upward leading, it should be taken thus, as it was also said previously regarding the little: 'it was good for him, if he had not been born.' Therefore, it is good for those more blessed, those who are still leading lives and those who have died, who have not yet been born.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The miscarriage came in vanity and walks in darkness because it never knew or did anything of human things, so it departs as it came.
comments.comment: Other people, when they are well-born and well-reared, having used the things given to them badly, had this vanity; but the miscarriage had even its very birth in vanity; it was conceived not that it might live, not that it might become a fetus, but that the womb might immediately perish, immediately as the conception occurred. In darkness, therefore, again, he did not come to men; he was not known, that 'in vanity he came and in darkness he walks' (Ecclesiastes 6:4). He did nothing, nor thought, nor knew anything of human things. And because of this, as he came with ignorance and through not having experienced these things, so again he walks. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is meant by coming in vanity and walking in darkness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The embryo that came in vain departs unnoticed, and this is lighter than the lot of the wicked man.
comments.comment: For as it [the untimely embryo] came in vain, so it departs unnoticed into oblivion, having touched no evils and never looked upon the sun (Ecclesiastes 6:4-5). This is lighter than the lot of the wicked man, even if he should measure out his life at a thousand years and not come to know goodness (Ecclesiastes 6:6). The end of both is death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words why the unborn is said to be better off.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The fool finds no fill for any desire, while the self-controlled man is not held by his passions.
comments.comment: The fool stands exposed above all in this, that he finds no fill for any desire (Ecclesiastes 6:7); but the self-controlled man is not held fast by these passions, and as a rule uprightness of life leads a person into poverty (Ecclesiastes 6:8). Spectacles for greedy eyes drive many out of their senses: they stir up the soul and drag it toward fruitless striving through the empty desire to be seen (Ecclesiastes 6:9).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the verses as a contrast between the fool's unfilled desire and the self-controlled man.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The life men lead here is a shadow, a consequence of an earlier and higher life, just as a shadow requires a body that casts it.
comments.comment:
This living we have while being in the flesh and passing through this. It is under time, it is under the number of days. But the truly living is eternal; and such a life is both eternal and without end. He speaks therefore about the life here, the life in heaven. And he made them in shadows; for who will announce to man what will be after him under the sun (Ecclesiastes 6:12). The life of men, which they lead here, is shadowy. …

It is impossible for a shadow to be without a pre-existing body. There must be a body so that a shadow may thus follow it. Therefore, the life here is a shadow, being a consequence of a preceding life, which the life occurring here follows. For this reason it is said, "our days are as a shadow." And Job also said previously, "the life of men on the earth is a shadow." The life on the earth, or the material life, the temporal, the one in the flesh, this is a "shadow" of the life above.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'shadow' of the verse: this life follows from a life above.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because this life is a shadow of another, a man should live by the life above it, and since no one can announce what follows him, all divination is refuted.
comments.comment:
So also the apostle, wishing to show the shadowy life, said, "If in this life we have only hoped, we are more to be pitied than all men" (1 Cor 15:19). Let a man, having some hope, attend to a shadow appearing to help him; in a palace, if someone perceives the face of a king not present, will the shadow or the appearance benefit him? For it is not possible for that which can be present to him beside a true king who rules according to laws, to be the shadow itself. Therefore our life is shadowy. But having known this, beloved, that this life is shadowy, attend to it as to something not permanent, as to something dependent on another; and in this, observe that there is another life which the shadowy life follows, and live and act according to that.

For thus "one is able to please God." Because of "who will announce to man" (Ecclesiastes 6:12) what follows him while he still exists under the sun, all divination is refuted from that source, all human prophecy. … And as I have said and now will say: we say that we have ignorance of the judgments of God, since they happen to be "unsearchable. The judgments of God are very deep" (Rom 11:33). And the abyss is incomprehensible or difficult to comprehend. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The things of men fall away, but if we become heavenly we will lift ourselves to God and be able to know what follows them.
comments.comment: Again, many among the rulers turned toward private interests. This same Ecclesiastes says: 'I saw slaves on horses and rulers riding about' (Eccl 10:7), and we cannot say for what reason he has this. But we can say in general that the things of men fall away. If, however, surpassing these, we become heavenly, no longer observing the temporal and apparent things, then we will lift ourselves to God, being able to know such things as follow after these.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The days we receive while surrounded by flesh are shadowy, while the true days are those of loving the Lord God.
comments.comment:
For each one receives a reward according to his practice and his work. This is said regarding God by the Psalmist: 'You will render to each according to his works' (Psalm 62:12). And even if the works are manifest, we do not trust in what kind of disposition is performing them. Moreover: 'And he made them in shadow.' The upward leading? He says this: 'Those having shone like the sun in the kingdom of their own Father' lived in the true days. In a manner of promising, he spoke concerning someone: 'I will fill him with length of days' (Psalm 91:16). Indeed, these long days occurring toward the light of the truth are not shadowy; they are the prototypes. But the days which we can still receive while surrounded by flesh are shadowy.

Then one knows 'in part,' when 'the perfection has not yet come' (1 Corinthians 13:10), when he possesses the 'earnest of the Spirit' (Eph 1:14) and the light of the truth. Someone 'made these days in shadow,' but he did not know what would be behind him, whether he would surpass the shadow or fall down by it. And so that we may take the view from another example: the Jews have come to be in shadow, 'in the shadow' of days, not in the days themselves. For Moses, speaking the previous and true days, interprets: 'This is your life and this is the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Love toward God does not lengthen days, for God-fearing men were quickly taken and mediocre men lived long.
comments.comment: But the love toward God occurring 'from all the soul and from all the disposition' does not work an increase of these days. For many diligent and God-fearing men were quickly transferred from life, and others, the most mediocre, lived long. For who will announce to man what will be behind him under the sun?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why no one can announce what will follow a man: God-fearing men die young and others live long.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question 'who will announce to man what will be after him' can be taken in two ways, and both are true.
comments.comment: One must take the word in two ways, so that this is both 'what shall be announced to him under the sun' (Ecclesiastes 6:12) and 'who else under the sun is able to announce'. Both are true. Furthermore, what is the leading up? This leading up is this: for both the man and the one striving to truly possess what is pleasant to him, it is asked 'who will announce to him, what will be after him under the sun'. It can be said here of the things that shine forth, those that lead up from the shadow, and those that guide from the temporal into the eternal. It is also possible to take this regarding the 'shadow' of righteousness, that 'who will announce to him, what will be to them under the sun', while still approaching righteousness. For he is no longer under the 'sun of righteousness' himself, having surpassed the shadow and having become in that truth seeing it 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Knowing the pleasant things to come gains a man nothing, yet curiosity still pries into what follows death.
comments.comment: A man who knows the pleasant things that will befall him in life gains nothing more by it, even if we grant that he knows them; and yet human curiosity still contrives to pry into what will happen even after each person's death, and to think it knows (Ecclesiastes 6:12). …
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the verse means: knowing the future gains nothing.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A name is good only when it is applied to a good thing, the oil stands for luxury, and the death through which the righteous die with Christ is better than a birth that joins the soul to evil.
comments.comment:
A good name is better than fine oil, and the day of death is better than the day of birth (Eccl 7:1). Names are not good or bad by their own nature; for they are composed of various letters, and no single letter is good or bad; but being applied to good things they are called good, and to evil things, evil. There, therefore, the good name signifies a good thing; yet Solomon says that nothing of the things that happen is good, except virtue and the knowledge of God.

But the oil now signifies luxury, which to those who live in luxury seems to be good. For that which is good by nature is called good, such as virtue, but to some, such as gold and silver. Thus also the rich man received his good things in his life, 'and Lazarus likewise the bad things' (Luke 16:25). But that oil is taken instead of luxury, David shows, saying concerning men that 'from the fruit of their grain and wine and oil they were filled' (Psalm 4:7).

If the praiseworthy death, through which the righteous die with Christ, is fit to dissolve the soul from evil and ignorance, so again the birth opposed to this death joins the soul to evil and ignorance; therefore such a death is preferable to such a birth.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The day of birth brings a man into a life of many evils, while the day of death puts an end to the struggling life.
comments.comment:
And the day of his death is preferred over the day of his birth. The day of birth is the beginning of tribulation and ill-doing. The day of birth introduces man into life, where there are many evils and bad things; but the day of death imposes an end upon the struggling life.

Therefore he who does not attend to the things at hand nor thinks great things upon them, but knowing that 'it is better to be dissolved with Christ' (κάλλιον ἀναλύσαντα σὺν Χριστῷ εἶναι), prefers the day of death over the day of birth. For the one is the beginning of many evils, but the other is the end and the description of the evils.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the day of death is called better than the day of birth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the house of mourning boasting and laughing are turned away, while the house of wine brings lust and songs.
comments.comment:
It is good to go into a house of mourning or to go into a house of wine (Ecclesiastes 7:2). Fluidity of character does not occur where mourning is. For there, boasting and laughing are turned away; this misfortune does not allow this to happen.

And at times, when we guard ourselves from misfortune through displeasure toward the unfortunate and the suffering, we are even permitted to appear joyful. But in the house of wine, what happens is contrary, bringing lust and songs, being a symptom of a coarse life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between the house of mourning and the house of wine.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mourning brings blessedness and is the beginning of comfort, but it is mourning for oneself or for others lost in sins, not for the one who has died.
comments.comment: But the ascent: the house is one of mourning, where there are doctrines of moral sins and the punishments upon them. For hearing these things, men both mourn and lament over themselves. So what, then, is the good in mourning? For it brings blessedness. For 'blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4). Mourning is a prelude and a beginning of comfort. But the Savior does not bless those who mourn in just any way. For sometimes they also fall away, even while the word says: 'Do not weep for one dead, nor mourn him; but weep with a weeping for the one departing from the presence of the Lord, because he will not return again' (Jeremiah 22:10). This one is worthy of weeping. It is not necessary to mourn the one dead, but the one dead having fallen away from blessedness and eternal life. In many ways, one can mourn himself having become lost in sins, if he perceives it. And he is blessed, the one mourning himself, having made himself worthy of mourning and having fallen from the blessed life, so that he may be comforted. And he mourns others also, when he is a lover of children. Thus indeed Paul was saying: 'Not having entered, I shall mourn many.' 'Many' he says, those 'not having repented.' This one mourning does not mourn himself, but the others having been made dead, or rather his own children through discipline in any way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who goes into the house of mourning knows that death is the end of every man, so he will not think great things of wealth, glory and rank, which he must cast off when he dies.
comments.comment: And the house signifies a certain state and an ascent, not a place. He knew this, the end of every man, and the living one will give good to his heart. The one going into a 'house of mourning' knows that 'the end of every man' is to die. And if he knows that he will die, he will not think much of it, nor will he consider it a matter of great importance if he possesses such things which he is able to cast off having died—wealth, glory, rank—according to 'do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, for he will not take all things in his dying' (Psalm 49:16-17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the house of mourning is good: it reminds a man of his end.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who truly lives, having the blessed life, finds good for his own soul, while the foolish man endures weeping even there.
comments.comment: Truly he finds 'good' for himself, 'entering into the joy of the Lord' (Matthew 25:21). But if he is foolish, there too he 'endures weeping' (Matthew 25:21). 'For there is the weeping and the gnashing of teeth' (Matt 8:12). And it is possible even to call the living 'the one living according to God'. Such were those around Abraham, concerning whom it has been said: 'God is not of the dead, but of the living' (Matt 22:32). The one truly living, the one having the blessed life, finds good for his own soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mourning is the end of man because the Lord blesses it.
comments.comment:
Blessedness is the end of man.

If the Lord blesses mourning in the Gospels: 'For blessed are they who mourn, for they shall be comforted' (Matt 5:4), then Solomon rightly says that mourning is the end of man, which fills those living in it with spiritual goods.
comments.selected_reason: Links the verse to the Lord's blessing on those who mourn.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A good anger, like a father's toward his child, is preferable to the laughter that finds pleasure in evils, and a threatened wrath comes before the punishment.
comments.comment:
… A good passion is over laughter, because in the wickedness of man he will be angry. And from what is at hand it is possible to see this: if anyone has obedient ones, such as children or slaves, when he thus becomes angry and is passionate toward them so as to prevent their wickedness, this 'passion' is 'good', not passion absolutely, but the father toward a child, the guardian toward those being cared for. 'Because in the wickedness of man he will be angry' (referring to the one seeking laughter, who becomes a fool there where the jesters are); but the one having 'passion' against those doing such things and will be angry for himself, whenever a calculation or a matter such as this comes to him, as we said recently, that he is angry for his own sake. … Having read the divine writings and having known how God is indignant against sinners and that he 'stirs up wrath' (Ps 7:11), which the holy man was entreating, saying: 'Do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger' (Psalm 6:1)—this wrath is not better than living with virtue; rather, if one is worthy to be punished, it is preferable for him to be rebuked through wrath or to be disciplined by that punishment. For he who is able to punish rages before the actual punishing.

Do we not hear in the Scripture that a threat lies in store against sinners? If the thing announced is wrath, what then is a threat? And in the threat is the wrath, not in the fulfillment of the threat. Or, in the punishment, is the wrath not greater? But he does not speak of this as a good thing, if anyone is tested by it, but rather that if wrath is released, sins increase, so that punishment may follow. Therefore, the 'good' is 'wrath over laughter.' That is, to find pleasure in evils. 'Because in the wickedness of man he shall be made good.' Laughter is made good in the wickedness of man; and the maker of laughter brings wickedness to himself and to others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who hunts for pleasures is made good in the wickedness of man, and his laughter only seems cheerful, while the heart of the wise is in a house of mourning.
comments.comment: Thus, he who hunts for pleasures is made good in the wickedness of man, he who prefers softness to a rigorous life. The face of this laughter seems to be cheerful in wickedness. But if we speak regarding the one being raged against, that the thing appearing in the threat is not a wickedness opposed to virtue, but a wickedness that punishes those who err, concerning which it is also written in the prophet Amos: 'If there is wickedness in the city, which the Lord did not make?' (Am 3:6). There is no evil occurring in a city by nature without God. The heart of the wise is in a house of mourning, and the heart of the foolish is in a house of mirth (Eccl 7:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sensible anger is preferred to laughter because a stern look sets the soul right.
comments.comment: Sensible anger is to be preferred to laughter, for by a stern look on the face the soul is set right (Ecclesiastes 7:3). So the souls of the wise are grave and hold themselves in, while the souls of fools are puffed up and run loose (Ecclesiastes 7:4).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear sense of why anger and gravity are preferred to laughter.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Anger that fights the demons for virtue is praiseworthy, and the righteous man prefers mourning and the rebuke of the wise to the mirth and flattery of fools.
comments.comment: When anger, striving for virtue, boxes with the demons, it is strong and praiseworthy; but when it contends with men over perishable things, it becomes trivial. Therefore, what he says here is such: that the fool is made good in wickedness and laughs and rejoices in it, neither rejecting shameful songs nor allowing laughter to corrupt his soul like the crackling of thorns in a fire; but the righteous man grows angry at such passions and is indignant, and considers it better to have mourning than such mirth, or the rebuke of a wise man against such songs; and he calls such a life vanity and flattery, easily deceiving the heart of the wise and dissolving its firmness in the virtues.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: False accusation is a great evil that plots against the steadfastness of the good, a speaker should be praised for how he ends, and anger must be kept in check.
comments.comment: This too is wretched, and indeed a very great evil: false accusation. It plots against the souls of the wise and tries to destroy the noble steadfastness of the good (Ecclesiastes 7:7). One should praise a speaker not as he begins his words but as he ends them, and welcome a modest character rather than one that is lofty and puffed up (Ecclesiastes 7:8). One must by all means keep anger in check and not be carried away readily into wrath, which fools serve as slaves (Ecclesiastes 7:9).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the oppression of 7:7 as false accusation and the 'end of a thing' as the end of a speech.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The first words of instruction are called words, but the last words are called words of works, for words are called good because of good works.
comments.comment: The last words are better than the first words of Creon, says the poet of the law, rather than the listener of the law (Eccl 7:8). For the first words of instruction are called words, but the last words are called words of works, if indeed words are called good words because of good works. Do not hasten in your spirit to be angry, for anger is in the belly of fools (Eccl 7:9).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The believer from the Gentiles is long-suffering, while those from the circumcision who say they have no king but Caesar are high in spirit.
comments.comment: Because you desire this: the one believing in the Savior from among the Gentiles is long-suffering, but the people from the circumcision who say, 'We have no king but Caesar' … and 'We are disciples of Moses' are high in spirit. Regarding this one who is high in spirit from the Hebrew people, the one from the Gentiles who became long-suffering because he has known the things concerning him—that 'having no hope and being without God in the world' (1 Thessalonians 4:13; Eph 2:12)—is a precursor there. Do not hasten in a spirit of anger, for anger rests in the foolishness of a mind in a rage.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Here 'bosom' stands for the soul.
comments.comment: It should be noted that here 'bosom' is used as a synonym for the soul; for no one would say that anger rests in the sensible bosom.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: A fool's passion rests in the heart, and the heart is in many places of the Scriptures the name for the ruling principle of a man.
comments.comment:
For a fool's passion rests in the heart. The one who is not a fool, but wise and attentive to prudence, even if something is ever seen or heard or moves the passion, it remains only until a passion occurs.

For the heart signifies the ruling principle in many of the divine lessons, as if it says: 'Their folly is in the land of Egypt in their heart' (Ps 106:27). So also it is said in other places that 'all things come into the heart of the unjust' (Prov 14:13). What he says is this: that he touches evils, and against his own ruling principle he brings harm and plague.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One should not ask why the former days were better, since the fear of the Lord adds days of holy knowledge, and what is ancient is not worthy of honor for its age alone.
comments.comment:
… do not say: 'What happened that the days that were before were better than these?' because you did not inquire about this in wisdom. If 'the fear of the Lord adds days' (Proverbs 10:27), it is for us to enjoy the good or better days of holy knowledge.

To think that things are given to the elders according to time and the first things of knowledge is not wise; for even if something is ancient, it is not necessarily worthy of honor, since even evil is ancient, but it is not worthy of being honored because of time, if 'not the long-lived are wise, nor do the elders understand judgment' (Job 32:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the question about the former days is called unwise.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The one who begins virtue and is enlightened by the sun of righteousness keeps stretching forward to what is before, as if to say that the first days were better than these.
comments.comment:
Do not say: 'What happened that the former days were better than these?' (Ecclesiastes 7:10). 'Better than these' is not merely said, but also reasoned: he who is beginning virtue and 'the illumination of the knowledge of truth' and being shone upon by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) always receives by the light; and just as the diligent man 'stretches toward the prize of the higher calling' (Phil 3:14).

The things being given are left behind, forgetting those from whom they have come, so that he no longer turns back and returns; 'stretching forward to those that are before' (Philippians 3:13), he is made distant, he who began to be enlightened by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) and always receives by the light, as if to say that 'the first days were better than these' (Ecclesiastes 7:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The question why the former days were better is not asked in wisdom, and the days of a man's life are to be understood as loving the Lord with all his heart, strength and soul.
comments.comment: He says this to himself, wondering, 'Why has this happened to me, that previously the days were good?' (Ecclesiastes 7:10) because he did not inquire about this in wisdom. The inquiry was in wisdom: 'Why, that I have received this?' I have become better than myself; they received something greater instead of something lesser. This, therefore, is praise, being the same as 'I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call' (Phil 3:14) … These days must be interpreted thus: 'This is your life and this is the length of your days: to love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your strength, and with all your soul' (Deut 6:5). This is the life of the ages, the length.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who praise the former times are mistaken, for wisdom surpasses money as silver outshines its shadow.
comments.comment: Those who say that a better life was granted to the people of former times are mistaken (Ecclesiastes 7:10). They do not understand that wisdom far surpasses an abundance of money, and is as much more conspicuous as silver shines brighter than its own shadow (Ecclesiastes 7:11-12). For a person's life comes not from acquiring perishable wealth but from wisdom (Ecclesiastes 7:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains that wisdom outshines money as silver outshines its shadow, and that life comes from wisdom.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Wisdom is good if it improves the soul and has its inheritance, for as no one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit, so no one is good in wisdom without its inheritance.
comments.comment:
Good wisdom with inheritance and abundance for those who look upon the sun. He says this: if this has become something improving the soul, approaching being in wisdom, it is good, if it possesses the inheritance. And I say: 'No one, he says, says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit' (1 Cor 12:3), even though many call him Lord, but not truly, not in truth. For he says to them: 'Why do you call me Lord, Lord, and do not do what I say? Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven' (Matt 7:21). This, therefore, is the one truly saying Lord Jesus through the participation of the Holy Spirit. The one having been persuaded of wisdom according to the Holy Spirit makes the wisdom of Jesus. And this one truly says Lord Jesus. Just as 'no one says Lord Jesus except in the Holy Spirit,' so no one is good in wisdom not having its inheritance.

… For they are wise in appearance only until they speak, but not until they act. The wisdom that follows inheritance is not that which is being made, and it carries the divine promise of becoming possessed by the wise. And there is abundance for those contemplating the sun.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who contemplate the sun may receive something more of the sun of righteousness, which is wisdom, and wisdom is in its shadow as the shadow of silver.
comments.comment:
Something more happens to those contemplating the sun, this sensible sun. We do not see the sun as other men do, but they receive a vision of greatness and beauty and knowledge, and from knowledge they become again able to understand who the sun of righteousness (Malachi 4:2) is. And it is possible for those contemplating the sun to receive something more of the sun of righteousness itself. This sun is the same as wisdom. For wisdom is in its shadow as the shadow of silver. That shadow of wisdom is that of the world.

And so that the geometric lines may be used by me as a scientific theorem, the shadows of knowledge are those lines. For those sensory contemplations lead toward knowledge. And regarding a shadow, he does not speak of a representation composed from a body having this form, but of the precedence of the icon. And the shadow of an icon is a certain enigmatic sketching.

Therefore, he who is about to take silver receives a shadow; I do not say a sensible thing, but the logos. For often this is also demonstrated, that silver is praiseworthy and refined according to the immediate context and the thing called 'the tongue of the righteous' (Proverbs 10:20). For when it is said, 'refined silver, the tongue of the righteous' (Proverbs 10:20), he calls the tongue of the righteous his silver.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who keep wisdom have more than those who received it and fell from it, who had acquired only a shadow of wisdom, as a man might acquire a shadow of silver and not silver.
comments.comment: Regarding 'good wisdom with inheritance, and abundance to those who behold the sun' (Eccl 7:11), and 'for wisdom is like the shadow of silver, and an abundance of knowledge will vivify the one beside it' (Eccl 7:12): just as those who behold the sun possess something more than those who have beheld it but no longer behold it, so those who happen to have wisdom and have authority over it have possessed something more—this is what is meant by 'with inheritance'—than those who received it and fell from it through their own lawlessness. For everyone who has acquired wisdom and lost it first acquired a shadow of wisdom and not wisdom, and later it seems as if a man had acquired a shadow of silver but had not acquired silver; for wisdom is by nature not something merely received, but it vivifies the one who possesses it through knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'shadow of silver' and 'inheritance' in the verses.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: No one can fully describe God's providence, so great and so kind.
comments.comment: Tell me, who will be able to describe in full the providence of God, so great and so kind? Or who will call back what God seems, and justly, to have left neglected (Ecclesiastes 7:13)?
comments.selected_reason: Reads the verse as about God's providence, which no one can describe in full.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The one called perverted is one who has turned aside, as when many meet the Scriptures and understand them as they ought not, through their own laziness.
comments.comment: Furthermore, how does he call the perversion? To demonstrate that he is such a person, one who has turned aside; for example, many encounter the Scriptures and understand them as they ought not to. And no one else turned them aside except their own laziness. When someone therefore demonstrates such a person, that 'do not pay attention to him; he speaks errantly, what he says,' he has shown him to be turned aside, he has demonstrated him to be such.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God made things so that man finds nothing of those who are to follow him, and the man who lives by sensation alone knows only the present, since it is the intellect that knows what follows.
comments.comment:
God made the world in such a way regarding speech, so that no man might find anything behind Him. … God made such a word in the things that exist, so that man might find nothing of those that are to follow him.

Here he invalidates human foreknowledge; man finds nothing of those who will receive him. And concerning human things he says: for the diligent man knows that he will receive a blessed state, which is clear everywhere. If not—if the human designation, being present, submits another through thought, and if he calls man not the mortal rational animal, but the one 'walking according to the flesh' and pleasures—such a man, being such, will not be recognized by those who are to follow, as long as he lives by sensation alone. For sensation recognizes only the present things. Since such a man is entirely of sensation, walking 'according to the flesh' and pleasures and other evils, he does not know the 'behind', the things that are to follow. For it is the intellect to know this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man may be righteous only in his own sense, and since every man seems righteous to himself, one must not remain in that righteousness, which destroys the one who has it.
comments.comment: In the days of my vanity, therefore, I saw all things. And 'the days of vanity' (Ecclesiastes 7:15) he means the days of this life, upon which he must not hope. For he prepares those who expect to be miserable. There is a righteous man perishing in his own righteousness; and there is an ungodly man remaining in his own wickedness. There is simply righteous, and there is someone's righteous. When therefore the Divine, in that word, says 'to pursue the righteous thing justly', he does not say to each one, 'pursue your own righteous thing justly', but the simply and principally righteous. Since every man seems righteous to himself and 'the last ways seem to be right to man, looking into the pits of Hades', one must not remain in that subjective righteousness. For he who has this destroys him, and he withholds from the one who has it. There is therefore a righteous man perishing in his own righteousness. But those who are righteous according to truth, about whom much has been written, such as: 'the righteous shall do in wealth many years' (Ps 112:9), these do not remain in their own righteousness; they do not trust in their own righteousness. Therefore he does not perish in righteousness, as the hymnodist says: 'in your righteousness I shall live' (Psalm 119:40).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that a righteous man perishes in his own righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man is not justified merely because he knows nothing against himself, and one who learns that his righteousness is not the truth perishes from it so that he may gain the truly righteous.
comments.comment:
It has become a matter of truth, he says: 'I do not know anything to myself, but not in this have I been justified.' For it enters into me, that I do not truly possess righteousness, and not because of this—that I have known nothing to myself of those things that harm—am I justified. And again the holy David says: 'If I saw iniquity in my heart, let not the Lord hear' (Psalm 66:18). A sign of having or not having iniquity is whether one is heard by God or not heard.

And it is possible also to take this in another way according to a second explanation: it is to cause someone to perish from his own righteousness; someone thinking himself righteous in his own righteousness, if... he knows that it is not the truth and the Lord of righteousness, he pulls himself away from this and perishes from his own righteousness. And this destruction does not corrupt. For just as we say of one departing from virtue that he has perished by virtue, so we say of one having changed from the presumption he formerly held, that he has perished from that presumption.

And there is an impious man remaining in his own wickedness, living in wickedness not recognizing his own wickedness, even though he was previously recognized as a righteous man before he was justifying himself. Is it then the same mind? That mind, even though being in righteousness, yet being less than the truly righteous, perishes from it, so that he may have the truly righteous. For example, let someone have a mistaken presumption, or let someone have a presumption that is not mistaken, but not in word, not in precision. If he knows the precision, he perishes himself, so that he may succeed in that intention by the better thing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The 'perishing' of the righteous man is called so as an abandonment through testing, as in the case of Job.
comments.comment: Regarding 'there is a righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and there is a godless man living in his wickedness' (Eccl 7:15-16), destruction is called so, as is the abandonment through testing, as in the case of Job: 'I have perished, for he says, and I have become a stranger' (Job 3:23).
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: He observed a righteous man holding to righteousness until death, and an ungodly man dying with his wickedness.
comments.comment: In earlier days, when I did not act rightly, I observed all things: a righteous man holding fast to righteousness and not turning from it even until death, and even plotted against because of it; and an ungodly man dying together with his own wickedness (Ecclesiastes 7:15).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the just man who perishes as one who holds to righteousness until death.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: One should not become excessively righteous or wise, nor become hard, for virtues are mediations and their excesses and deficiencies are wickednesses.
comments.comment: Do not become much righteous and do not philosophize excessively, lest you be struck with amazement. Do not be impiously much and do not become hard, so that you do not die not in your time (Ecclesiastes 7:16). And it has been said to us many times, that virtues are mediations, while their excesses and deficiencies are wickednesses.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the warning against going to excess in righteousness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who chooses evil becomes hard, as in Pharaoh's heart, having an unrepentant heart that stores up wrath.
comments.comment: And do not become hard. He who chooses evil becomes hard. For he constructs hardness for the one possessing it. 'For according to your hardness and your unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath' (Rom 2:5). You see that: having an unrepentant heart, one is found hard. And thus it happens to the heart of Pharaoh, which has been written of many times, having been hardened. 'Do not be excessively wise, do not become hard, so that you do not die in your time' (Ecclesiastes 7:16-17).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must be neither too righteous nor impious, for an impious thought makes the soul die in ignorance, as the Sodomites died at their inopportune time, while he who fears God emerges from every evil.
comments.comment:
Do not become too righteous, and do not philosophize excessively, lest you be struck with amazement (Eccl 7:16). Do not be impiously excessive and do not become harsh, so that you do not die at an inopportune time (Eccl 7:17). It is good that you hold fast to this, and indeed do not withdraw your hand from this, for he who fears God will emerge from all things (Eccl 7:18). Do not let an impious thought be lodged in your heart, lest your soul, having been impious, die in ignorance. The Sodomites and the Gomorrites died at their inopportune time (Gen 19). And if this time is a time of uprightness, those dying in this time and being separated from the life that is to come—'I am the life' (John 14:6)—do not die at an inopportune time.

It is good that you hold fast to not being too righteous, and indeed do not withdraw your heart from impiety, for fearing God, he will emerge from every evil.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: The righteous should not seem excessively righteous or wise, for the greatest good is to lay hold of God, and the fear of God escapes every adversity.
comments.comment: If you are righteous, you should not appear exceedingly so, nor too wise, beyond measure, lest you stumble somewhere and sin many times over (Ecclesiastes 7:16). Do not be bold and rash, lest an untimely death snatch you away (Ecclesiastes 7:17). The greatest good is to lay hold of God and, remaining in this, to commit no sin. For to touch what is undefiled with an unclean hand is an abomination. He who submits with the fear of God escapes every adversity (Ecclesiastes 7:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the warning against being righteous over much and what it is to 'take hold of this'.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: One is to hold fast and persist in the virtues, for practice brings progress in them, as practice brings temperance and justice, in which one remains.
comments.comment:
It is good to hold fast to this, and not to let go of your hand from it. In each of the things said, you heard: do not become very righteous; hold fast to this. It has said, 'Do not be excessively wise.' In all the things said, hold fast as if in one genus.

Therefore, from what I have said, that it is also necessary to hold fast, do not let your practice cease. Persist in them, as the apostle says: 'Hold these things, be in these, so that your progress may become evident' (1 Tim 4:15), in the virtues. Meditating on these, it is necessary to remain in them, not to depart further from them. … Let us take it. It is not good to remain in the study of characters, but to run quickly toward the next progress. Regarding virtues, practice brings progress: practice brings temperance, and one remains in temperance; practice brings justice, and one remains in justice; for in this way one is able to be shown to be diligent.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who fears God comes out of all things in the sense of reaching their end and outcome, and the fear meant is not the fear of punishment.
comments.comment:
For he who fears God will come out of all things (Ecclesiastes 7:18). Even if you have much help—help for coming out—it does not say that he becomes outside of all things. But 'to come out' signifies the end and the outcome, as we say that the holy voices that occurred regarding the coming of the Savior have attained an outcome. And this is 'so that it might be fulfilled' (Matthew 2:15). For those from the heterodox, either maliciously or through ignorance, think that this fulfillment is to be taken in this way: that it might be fulfilled so that it might not be empty. And they say that the Old Testament was empty in itself and required fulfillment from without. Not this, but he speaks regarding an outcome: because of this Mary gave birth, 'so that it might be fulfilled; behold, she shall hold in her womb' (Matthew 1:23). Because of this the Savior was crucified, because of 'they have pierced my hands and my feet' (Ps 22:16). He who fears God does not become outside of them, but reaches their end.

This is similar to what the apostolic text says: 'not of him who runs nor of him who wills, but of God who shows mercy' (Rom 9:16). Therefore, he who fears God 'comes out of all things' (Ecclesiastes 7:18). For 'the fear of the Lord surpasses all things' (Sirach 25:11). And if it surpasses all things, 'there is nothing above him.' For it is not the fear of punishment that is spoken of, but that one, about whom we say: 'there is no lack to those who fear him' (Ps 34:9). And 'He' is God. For He says: 'be holy to Him, for He is your fear' (Isaiah 8:13). Just as the one desiring wisdom becomes wisdom in Christ, and the righteousness of the righteous becomes righteousness in Christ, so also fear becomes so.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since all things are governed by the will of God, even things that seem to happen humanly, such as wealth or rule, are a gift from God.
comments.comment: Wisdom will help the wise, while those exercising authority in the city are being overcome. … For according to the true word, since all things are governed by the will of God, even things that seem to happen humanly are a gift from God. To have wealth is human, but 'the Lord makes rich' (1 Sam 2:7); to have the beginning is human, but the Lord 'establishes kings and deposes them' (1 Sam 2:7). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even many powerful men cannot help a city without wisdom, and the same holds for the world, which is called a city, and for each soul, which can be called a city.
comments.comment:
Since he who says these things is most especially a king, he anoints all things toward piety; he says this because even if there are ten in authority in the city, and many are helping, and they surpass the opponents in number and power, if they do not have wisdom, they are not able to help the city.

Therefore, always seek the power of this general in his wisdom rather than in the multitude of his array.

"So then wisdom will help the wise one among the ten exercising authority in the city."

What is at hand to us has been given regarding history. If a city has many powerful men, but wisdom is lacking, they are not able to help the city.

And for the sake of an analogy, the world, the place around us, is called a city. If divine wisdom is not given, no one is able to pass through safely.

If wisdom does not help, those in authority can do nothing, even if they should be angels or holy men. If wisdom does not help, the city is not saved.

And each person's soul can also be called a city. If indeed someone has a myriad of human thoughts capable of helping this city, but divine wisdom does not help it and lead it and guard it toward the lawful, it is not able to be helped.

And observe "those who are in the city." You know that many times authority is taken from without. And you have in the histories of the Scriptures that many times those who were acting against Israel and its kings hired other kings.

But the ones hired from without do not contribute to helping the city as the natives do. Indeed, when they see that the matter is weak, they withdraw and are favorable toward the opponents.

"Therefore, those who are in the city"; even if they are rich and are well-disposed toward it and are even well-prepared for this very thing, to help the city, in the absence of wisdom they are not able to endure what is urgent.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how wisdom helps a city, and how 'city' can mean the world or the soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom helps a city more than the mightiest men, and justly pardons those who stumble.
comments.comment: Wisdom can give greater help than a band of the mightiest men in a city (Ecclesiastes 7:19), and it often justly pardons those who fall short of what they ought to do; for there is not one who never stumbles (Ecclesiastes 7:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains that wisdom pardons those who stumble, since there is no one who never stumbles.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The verse says a man is not righteous in the land, meaning the man who walks according to the flesh and sets his mind on earthly things, and no such man is righteous.
comments.comment: For man is not righteous in the land (Ecclesiastes 7:20). He did not say at once that a man is not righteous, but in the land. … The man on earth is the one 'walking according to the flesh' (Rom 8:4), according to 'you indeed die as men' (Psalm 82:7). This one is on earth not only in body, but also in heart. He 'sets his mind on earthly things' (Philippians 3:19), and 'sinks himself into his seat'. No one of such people is righteous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'on earth' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Taken as plain history the verse would mean that no man born on earth is without sin, but not every sin harms the one who does it, as a painter learning his art draws many icons badly so that he may learn to draw well.
comments.comment:
I say 'man' not simply, but the one not being on earth who is able to be righteous. 'If one walks on earth, having his portion in heaven', he is wise not on earth. Because of this, the one having righteousness is not prevented from being called a lawbreaker from it. Furthermore, why do you not stand according to history? If you wish to take it according to history, you descend into a dogma, that there is no man born on earth without sin.

I said, that this brings us labor regarding John and regarding this Jeremiah, unless indeed you take that sin, according to which it has been said: 'all have sinned' (Rom 3:23). You know, however, that I once omitted this and said that not every sin brings harm to the one doing it, when I also use an icon such as this, that a painter is learning the art: many icons are drawn not well, and this sin bringing them is not a mockery. Because of this, he draws not well, so that he may learn to draw well. And many things must be done sinfully, so that someone might thus correctly achieve the goal of his work.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One should give the ungodly no hearing, lest stung by what is said against oneself one curses in return.
comments.comment: Give the words of the ungodly no hearing at all, so that you do not hear with your own ears what is said against you, like the chatter of a wicked slave, and then, stung to the heart, you too later turn aside in many of your dealings to curse in return (Ecclesiastes 7:21-22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why one should not listen to every word: so as not to curse in return.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Having cast away the wisdom received from God, he found it fled to an unmeasured depth.
comments.comment: I came to know all these things when I received wisdom from God; but later I cast it away, and was no longer able to be as I had been (Ecclesiastes 7:23). For wisdom fled from me to an endless distance and an unmeasured depth, so that it could no longer be grasped (Ecclesiastes 7:24).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the verses as the Preacher's loss of the wisdom he had received from God.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: When he desired to receive wisdom it became far from him beyond what it was before, and the words 'who will find it?' may mean 'no one'.
comments.comment: This also Solomon says concerning wisdom: 'I said, I will be wise, and it was lengthened far beyond what it was, and a deep depth, who will find it?' (Ecclesiastes 7:23-24). It was far from me, and when I desired to receive it, it became far from me beyond what it was before. And therefore he gives the reason: 'a deep depth, who will find it?' The 'who will find' may mean 'no one.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who circles the whole cosmos and sees all that God made sees it as very beautiful, and having grasped all things together in thought, wisdom finds the truth.
comments.comment:
Furthermore: the ascent. Did I encircle it to know? It is a whole ascent; we say this. It is not far from what was said, that, since 'the maker of them is seen through the greatness of beauty and of creatures' (Wisdom 13:5), the one circling the whole cosmos and seeing all that God made, sees them as 'very beautiful' (Gen 1:31). But if he does not circle, but takes one by one, he does not see the beauty of the created. …

By knowing the creation, one knows the Creator, according to His power. Then, having grasped all things together in thought as if circling, wisdom finds the truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Having given up seeking wisdom, he was carried away by a deadly desire and came to know the woman.
comments.comment: So afterward I gave up even seeking it altogether, and no longer gave thought to examining the follies of the ungodly, their vain counsels, and their aimless life (Ecclesiastes 7:25). Being in this state, I was carried away into those very things; and gripped by a deadly desire, I came to know the woman, who is a kind of earth, or something else of that sort (Ecclesiastes 7:26).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The wicked woman has not one snare but many, with a bond in her hands, and the sinless are not caught by her but are outside her, trampling her.
comments.comment: So also here the wicked woman called here—whether you mean regarding rhetoric or regarding opinion—does not have one snare. When you think you have escaped one, she lays another. A bond is in her hands. She immediately binds the one approaching. Her hand refers to practice and energy. The one acting according to her is not only hunted and snared, but also falls into a bond; he is judged a prisoner. The good man will be taken out from her before the face of God. The good man before the face of God is not such in essence, but the one hurrying to have virtue, so that he may become even more good for God. This one, therefore, does not fall into her, is not hunted, is not snared. But the foolish one is handed over to the good man 'not falling into her snares' or into the bonds. And 'being handed over' is often interpreted: after many times preventing, when that evil no longer prevents, a handing over to him occurs. And he will be caught sinning in her. No one sinless is caught by her. The beginning of being caught is having sinned. Indeed, it approaches even the saints; but since they do not sin, they are not caught by her, but are outside her, trampling her.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What the Preacher found is that the woman has snares in her heart and a bond in her hand, and he found it not from himself but because God revealed to him the cunning of this thought.
comments.comment:
'Behold, I have found this,' says the Preacher (Eccl 7:27), 'one single thought to find, which my soul sought and did not find.' The Preacher is the teacher of the general assembly. 'The Preacher found this'—the 'finding' here is 'grasping.' But what kind? This very thing: that the woman who exists has snares in her heart and a bond in her own hand. To know this is of the Preacher. For this will benefit those listening to the Preacher.

Regarding 'one single'—since he speaks here in the plural; for it is not spoken about only one alone, that 'one single.' We mean, that is, about her snares; he says that her deceits and her snares find a foolish thought and teach it. For indeed, these women also mislead one another and lead forward not toward finding a good thought, but toward being cunning. But did he not say 'one' above? The evil is not single, but rather many and widely spread.

Listen closely, for he does not say these things about a specific woman, but about every woman having such zeal, 'one single thought to find.' And if you take it regarding the snares, you say that even the snares seem to be in agreement. For those professing false doctrines attempt to say that their false opinions agree. 'Which my soul sought and did not find.' My soul sought their thought, and did not find it. It is difficult to hunt. It is like the things said: 'Do we not ignore His thoughts?' (Job 11:6) 'Who could enter to strike His armor?' (Job 41:13).

But what then is the 'found' in the preceding? Here he says additionally: 'one single thought to find.' This thought I desired to see, so that I might also teach them. And 'did not find' can be said in such a way as 'not of the one willing nor the one running, but of the God who shows mercy.' From myself I found nothing. But God revealed to me; He showed me the cunning of this thought.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He sought chastity among all women and found it in none.
comments.comment: I sought chastity among all women and found it in none (Ecclesiastes 7:27-28). One might find a chaste man among a thousand, but not a woman (Ecclesiastes 7:28).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Men made simple by God draw intricate reasonings upon themselves.
comments.comment: This above all I perceived: that human beings, made simple in their souls by God, draw upon themselves intricate reasonings and endless inquiries, and, while pretending to seek wisdom, wear themselves out over petty words (Ecclesiastes 7:29).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'many inventions' as intricate reasonings and endless inquiries.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A wise man can be recognized only by someone who knows the wisdom that made him wise, as a shipbuilder is known only by one who knows the art of building ships.
comments.comment:
Who knows the wise? And who knows the resolution of a sentence? Wisdom illuminates a man's face. He who understands the wise is rare. For it is a matter of knowing scientifically who is wise. …

No one can know a shipbuilder without examining the art by which he constructs ships. … so it is not possible to know a wise man without having known the wisdom by which he has become wise and by which he is called wise. Surely, others recognize others, and others do not recognize others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wisdom that makes a man's face shine is the light of his inner man, not of his body, and it is the light that Christ gives.
comments.comment:
This says that the wisdom of man shows his face to be luminous, not the face of the body, nor the member of the flesh, but the face of the inner man, about which the wise say: 'The light of your face has been shone upon us, Lord' (Psalm 4:6). …

In your face there is light—for your word is your image, your character—the one participating in this light is enlightened and becomes illuminated. Thus Jesus says to those who drew near to him: 'Let your light shine before men' (Matt 5:16). And he says to all: 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14). The apostles are not a light perceptible to the world, that is, visible to the many of men, but of the true world. … This, therefore, is the face of the inner man being enlightened by wisdom. And wisdom, light, word, truth, and the other notions called concerning Christ are the same.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the shining face means, in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The shameless man, who lacks the boldness that comes from wisdom, is hateful even when no one hates him.
comments.comment: And the shameless one will be hated before his face. … The shameless one, the one not having boldness from the light and wisdom that is absent, will be hated as a reproof. This exists especially for the sophists who wish to philosophize the truth. For from much shamelessness they argue against the truth. … Therefore he is hateful, even if he sometimes escapes through craftiness and is not hated, but indeed he is hateful. And he is hateful who is worthy of being hated, even if no one hates him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bright face is one with no covering of ignorance or wickedness.
comments.comment: Where the face is revealed from ignorance and sin; for 'the wisdom of man brightens his face' (Ecclesiastes 8:1). This bright face does not have a covering of ignorance, nor an overlay of wickedness, but is pure …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wisdom that makes a man's face shine is the light that saves his inner man, enlightened by the glory of the Lord.
comments.comment: The light is the salvation of your inner man, concerning which it is said: “The wisdom of a man makes his face shine” (Ecclesiastes 8:1). And again the saint says to have “the eyes of the heart” (Eph 1:18) enlightened, and “with an unveiled face to reflect the glory of the Lord” (2 Cor 3:18). When the face is reflected by the appropriate and divine glory and is enlightened by wisdom, God is my salvation. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Divine knowledge is the wisdom of God and enlightens the one who has it, while those full of ignorance wander in darkness.
comments.comment: The divine knowledge, being wisdom of God, shines and enlightens the one having it; for the wisdom of man enlightens his face (Ecclesiastes 8:1), and those called toward divine knowledge have the command to enlighten for themselves the light of knowledge. If then the wise according to God happen to be enlightened, those who are contrary, being filled with ignorance and unreasonableness, wander in darkness, always progressing in evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom shows in a person's face, and one must heed the king's words and avoid every oath.
comments.comment: When wisdom is tested in a person, it shines out even through the face, lighting up the one who possesses it (Ecclesiastes 8:1); just as shamelessness, the moment its owner is seen, proves the one in whom it has made its home worthy of hatred. One must pay very careful heed to the words of the king, and avoid an oath in every way, above all one made in the name of God (Ecclesiastes 8:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how wisdom shows in the face, and reads the oath of God as a warning against swearing.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The mouth of the king is the word of the king of truth, to be kept in life and thought, and no oath is to be taken hastily.
comments.comment: 'Guard the mouth of a king' (Ecclesiastes 8:2). Guard the mouth of the king of the truth; keep his word, live and think according to his word. For the mouth has often been demonstrated to us to signify the word. … And do not be hasty regarding the word of the oath of God. And among those outside, such a thing is hateful. He who is hasty to swear provides a ground for suspicion, unless an oath is imposed upon him by the ruler in the absence of any witness and he is compelled to swear concerning this. Therefore he said: 'Do not be hasty,' meaning: do not take a voluntary course toward swearing; do not handle an unprovable faith. If it is possible for faith to be provided, do not be hasty regarding an oath.
comments.selected_reason: Says whose mouth is meant and what the warning about oaths means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Mouth' here means the word.
comments.comment: Guard the mouth of a king (Ecclesiastes 8:2). Now 'mouth' refers to the word or the commandment.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: One should guard against every evil word and blasphemy, since God's decrees cannot be faulted, and it is better to hold to the holy commandments.
comments.comment: Even so, one should keep watch over an evil word, but guard against all blasphemy toward the Master (Ecclesiastes 8:3). For when he inflicts anything, there will be no finding fault, nor any speaking against the decrees of the only Sovereign and King (Ecclesiastes 8:4). It is better and more profitable to hold fast to the holy commandments and to stand clear of evil words (Ecclesiastes 8:5). For a wise man knows and foresees the judgment that comes in its time, that it will be just.
comments.selected_reason: Reads the king of these verses as God, whose decrees no one may fault.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
