comments.capsule: He who keeps the commandment does not set himself toward an evil word, because one who knows the good word also understands its opposite.
comments.comment: 'He who keeps the commandment will not know an evil word' (Ecclesiastes 8:5), that is, he will not set himself toward an evil word, the evil word being known by knowledge to the one guarding the divine commandment, which is the word of God; for since there is one knowledge of opposites, he who knows the good word also understands its opposite.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'will not know an evil word' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All human affairs await punishment from above, and no one can set aside the hour of death.
comments.comment: For all the affairs of human life await the punishment that comes from above (Ecclesiastes 8:6); but the wicked man does not seem to understand well that, since great providence watches over him, nothing whatever will escape notice in time to come. For he does not know what is coming, and no one will be able to declare any of it as it deserves (Ecclesiastes 8:7); for no one will be so strong as to be able to hinder the angel who takes away his soul, nor could any means at all be found to set aside the hour of death. Rather, like a man caught in the middle of a battle, one sees on every side what cannot be escaped; and all a man's ungodliness perishes with him (Ecclesiastes 8:8).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reading of what the verses say about judgment and death.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: People devise many ways to harm their neighbors, and the wicked sin all the more because God's forbearance does not punish at once.
comments.comment: I am astounded whenever I see what sort of things, and how many, people have devised to harm their neighbors (Ecclesiastes 8:9). And I know that the ungodly are snatched away from here before their time and removed from the scene, because they had given themselves over to vanity (Ecclesiastes 8:10). For since God's providence, in its great forbearance, does not swiftly pursue everyone, nor punish offenses on the spot, the wicked man supposes for this reason that he ought to sin all the more, as though he will get off unpunished (Ecclesiastes 8:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why sinners are emboldened when judgment is slow.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Even after a very long time a wrong is not overlooked, and the greatest good is to revere God.
comments.comment: He does not understand that even after a very long time the wrong he has done will not go unnoticed (Ecclesiastes 8:12). Yet the greatest good is to revere God; the ungodly man who has fallen away from this will not long have the use of his own folly (Ecclesiastes 8:12-13).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The good promised to those who fear God is the knowledge of God, and the vanity is that the righteous receive what belongs to the impious and the impious what belongs to the righteous.
comments.comment: For even I know that it will be good for those fearing God, so that they may fear from his face (Eccl 8:12); and it will not be good for the impious, and he who does not fear from the face of God will not prolong his days in the shadow (Eccl 8:13). Now 'good' refers to the knowledge, the knowledge of God. It is vanity which has been made upon the earth (Ecclesiastes 8:14), that if they are righteous, it comes to them as a work of the impious, and if they are impious, it comes to them as a work of the righteous; I said that even this is vanity. …
comments.selected_reason: Says what the good of 8:12 is and what the vanity of 8:14 is.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: People often hold a false opinion that reverses the just and the unjust, and he counts this among the most grievous errors.
comments.comment: A very bad and false opinion often spreads among people about the just and the unjust. For they suppose the reverse about each: one man who was just was not thought to be so, and again an ungodly man was held to be wise (Ecclesiastes 8:14). For my part, I count this error among the most grievous.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: He once thought eating and drinking the greatest good, and learned that a man mired in such things can never find what is truly good.
comments.comment: I once thought that the greatest of goods was eating and drinking, and that the man dearest to God was the one who enjoyed these things in life as much as he possibly could (Ecclesiastes 8:15). I held that such good cheer was the only comfort of life, and so I attended to nothing else but this notion, so that neither by night nor by day did I keep myself away from anything people have discovered for luxury (Ecclesiastes 8:16). And I learned this much: that someone who mires himself in those things will never be able, not even with much toil, to find what is truly good (Ecclesiastes 8:17).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how this reading takes the verses on eating and drinking.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: He once thought that all people were counted worthy of the same things, so that the wise man's care for righteousness seemed to be labor in vain.
comments.comment: For at that time I thought that all people were counted worthy of the same things; and if any wise man cared for righteousness, turned away from injustice, and avoided enmity by dealing graciously with everyone, which is pleasing to God, he seemed to labor in vain (Ecclesiastes 9:1). One end seemed to belong to the righteous and the ungodly, the good and the bad, the clean and the unclean, the one who seeks God's favor and the one who does not (Ecclesiastes 9:2). For when the unjust man and the good, the perjurer and the one who shuns every oath, were expected to be driven toward the same end, a kind of condemning verdict crept in: that all come to a like end (Ecclesiastes 9:3).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the opening verses read as a view he once held.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The belief that the dead are wholly gone and that the living are to be preferred is, he says, the reasoning of fools, error and deception.
comments.comment: But now I know that these are the reasonings of fools, errors and deceptions. They say many things: that the one who has died is wholly gone, and that the living man is to be preferred to the dead, even if he lies in darkness, even if he goes through life like a dog, over the lion that is dead (Ecclesiastes 9:4). "For the living at least know this, that they will die; but the dead know nothing at all (Ecclesiastes 9:5). No recompense for anything lies ahead once a man has met his fated end. Both the hatred and the love felt toward the dead come to an end. For whatever zeal they had has failed; whatever life they had has vanished. One who has once departed from here has a share in nothing (Ecclesiastes 9:6)."
comments.selected_reason: Explains how these verses are taken as a mistaken view.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Error urges a man to live in luxury and do whatever lies at hand, since no one will demand an account and Hades has no share in wisdom.
comments.comment: Still chanting these spells, Error gives advice like this: "What are you doing, my man? Why are you not living in luxury, gorging yourself on every kind of food and filling yourself with wine beyond measure (Ecclesiastes 9:7)? Do you not see that these things have been given by God for enjoyment without hindrance? Put on freshly washed clothes, anoint your head with perfume, and look at this woman, and at that one, and pass your vain life in vain (Ecclesiastes 9:8-9). For nothing else is left to you besides these things, neither here nor after death. Rather, do whatever lies at hand (Ecclesiastes 9:10). For no one will demand from you an account of these things, and what human beings do is not known at all outside of human beings. And Hades, whatever it may be, where we are said to go, has no share in wisdom or perception (Ecclesiastes 9:10)." That is what the vain say.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Solomon's bright garments are not a call to revel in fine clothes but a picture of a life washed clean of all filth.
comments.comment: Solomon too writes somewhere: ‘At all times let your garments be bright’ (Ecclesiastes 9:8). I would say that our wise Solomon, who understood very rightly, would not go so far in trifling as to urge us to revel childishly in bright clothes; rather, he likens to a bright robe the life that is, so to speak, washed clean and free from all filth. Otherwise, how could anyone put on our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:14)? Would you not say, my friend, that one who is clothed in the glories of the gospel way of life surely achieves just that?
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the bright garments mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 14

comments.capsule: The command to keep the garments white is about the garments of the inner man, not bodily pleasures.
comments.comment: For the Holy Spirit does not teach regarding bodily pleasures to such an extent as to think so, but rather regarding garments that clothe and adorn the inner man, about which it is commanded in Ecclesiastes: 'Let your garments always be white' (Eccl 9:8), which God himself clothes and endows the soul that speaks thankfully: 'I will rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and the robe of gladness' (Isaiah 61:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The swiftest will not finish the great race nor the mighty win the war, wealth does not bring understanding, and those who think all meet one lot will suddenly receive the penalty they deserve.
comments.comment: But I know well that those who seem swiftest will not finish that great race, and those reputed among men as mighty and fearsome will not win the fearful war; nor is prudence proved by an abundance of food, nor does understanding usually keep company with wealth (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Nor do I share the gladness of those who think that all people will meet the same lot (Ecclesiastes 9:11). Those who ponder such things seem to be fast asleep. They do not reckon that, snatched away like fish and birds, they will be worn down in misfortunes, suddenly receiving the penalty they deserve (Ecclesiastes 9:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the two verses in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A small city is great if it has even one wise citizen, though poor, who could save it, yet others do not recognize him.
comments.comment: But I hold wisdom so great a thing that even a small city, inhabited by few and besieged by the hand of a great king, I count populous and great if it has even one wise citizen, though he is poor (Ecclesiastes 9:13–15). For such a man could save his own city both from the enemy and from the siege works. Others do not recognize that poor wise man (Ecclesiastes 9:15) …
comments.selected_reason: Shows the point of the story of the poor wise man.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The strength of wisdom is preferred to common power, and though wisdom with poverty is despised now, it will be heard afterward.
comments.comment: I much prefer the strength that lies in wisdom to this common sort of power (Ecclesiastes 9:16). Here, it is true, wisdom that lives with poverty is held in dishonor (Ecclesiastes 9:16); but afterward it will be heard, its voice rising above rulers and tyrants who reach for evil (Ecclesiastes 9:17). For wisdom is stronger even than iron; and the folly of one man brings danger on many, even if many despise it (Ecclesiastes 9:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains that the poor man's wisdom, despised now, will be heard afterward.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Flies spoil sweet ointment, and wisdom and folly cannot be mentioned in the same breath, for the wise man goes to the right and the fool to the left.
comments.comment: For flies that fall into ointment and drown in it make both the look and the use of that sweet anointing unsightly (Ecclesiastes 10:1); but it is not fitting to make any mention of wisdom and folly in the same breath. The wise man guides himself to the right in his affairs, but the fool has turned aside to the left (Ecclesiastes 10:2), and there is never a time when he will use folly as a guide to good things. Even his thoughts are empty, filled with folly (Ecclesiastes 10:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the flies and the right and left hand in plain terms.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The wise man's heart is at his right because he fixes his mind on spiritual things, while the fool's is at his left among material things.
comments.comment: And in Ecclesiastes, in praise of the right, it is said thus: 'The heart of the wise is at his right hand, but the heart of a fool is at his left' (Ecclesiastes 10:2). The wise man, having his mind upon the intelligible and spiritual things, is called right because the precious things are on the right; but he who lacks understanding regarding sensible and material things is second and on the left.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the right and the left are used.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Passions left unrebuked grow worse and lead to ruin, so one must rebuke what is base and not leave one's place.
comments.comment: [Of the "spreading rash" that barred a man from the priesthood, Leviticus 21:20:] The spreading rash, besides, is any passion at all that keeps creeping outward over a wider area and never stops growing worse. But the divine law wants us to check the passions that befall us and to reduce them. You will understand something of this kind when you hear: ‘If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place, for healing will put an end to great sins’ (Ecclesiastes 10:4). For passions left unrebuked always creep toward a more shameful state; they seize heart and mind and lead to utter ruin. So we must rebuke what is base …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Stand firm against a hostile spirit, knowing God can pardon many sins.
comments.comment: If ever a hostile spirit should fall upon you, my friend, stand firm against it with strength, knowing that God is able to pardon even a great multitude of sins (Ecclesiastes 10:4). …
comments.selected_reason: Reads the ruler's spirit as a hostile spirit to be resisted, trusting in God's pardon.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The tyrant raises the fool, brings the prudent low, and lets slaves ride while holy men walk.
comments.comment: These are the works of a tyrant and of the father of all wickedness: that the fool is raised on high and the man rich in prudence is brought low (Ecclesiastes 10:5–6); that slaves of sins are seen riding on horseback, while holy men go on foot in dishonor, as the wicked exult (Ecclesiastes 10:7).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the reversals of 10:5-7 are read.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A man who plots against another lays an ambush for himself.
comments.comment: If anyone plots against another, he fails to see that he is laying an ambush first and only for himself (Ecclesiastes 10:8). The man who tears down another's security will fall prey to a serpent's bite (Ecclesiastes 10:8). Moreover, the man who quarries stones will bear no small toil, and the man who splits wood also carries danger in his very own tool (Ecclesiastes 10:9). If the axe happens to leap from its handle, the man at this work will be thrown into confusion (Ecclesiastes 10:10); he gathers to no good end, and he himself increases his own unjust and short-lived power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the proverbs about pits, hedges and axes.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The fool is ruined by his own chatter, while the good man does good to his neighbors.
comments.comment: A serpent's bite comes unseen; the charmers will bring no comfort, for they are useless (Ecclesiastes 10:11). But the good man does good both to himself and to his neighbors, while the fool will fall into ruin through his own chatter (Ecclesiastes 10:12). Once he opens his mouth, he begins foolishly and soon stops, showing his own senselessness at every turn (Ecclesiastes 10:13–14).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The idle ruin a house, and gluttons do shameful things for small pay.
comments.comment: The sluggish and the idle bring a house to decline, turning into mockers (Ecclesiastes 10:18). Squandering everything on their own gluttony, easily led by silver, they stoop to doing anything, shamefully and basely, for the sake of a small price (Ecclesiastes 10:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the idle ruin a house and what the love of money leads them to do.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: One should obey rulers and never fling a wounding word at them, since private words may come out.
comments.comment: It is right to obey a king, rulers, or men in power, and not to make oneself hateful to them, nor to fling any wounding word at them at all. For there is reason to fear that what is said even in private may somehow come into the open (Ecclesiastes 10:20). For to the only King, rich and great, swift and winged angels carry everything, performing a service at once spiritual and rational.
comments.selected_reason: Plainly says why one should not speak ill of rulers.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The command to send bread upon the waters is not about bread in the literal sense, and 'water' stands for the multitude of men to whom the bread of salvation is sent.
comments.comment:
… 'Send your bread upon the face of the waters, for in the multitude of days you will find it; divide it to the seven and also to the eight' (Eccl 11:1ab2a). This wording has nothing to do with the literal. For what is useful for history is the 'bread' which someone has, to send 'upon the face of the waters'? Rather, it makes it useless. Therefore, this wording must be taken for thought alone and for spiritual ascent.

Often in the abundance of divine teachings, the multitude of men is addressed by this name: 'Save me,' he says, 'from many waters, from the hand of the sons of strangers'; 'many waters' has spoken of the 'sons of strangers' of the divine wrath. And again there are many other writings teaching this; it is indeed said that 'God gives upon the water...' and they are not found to be taken according to history. But the multitude of men can signify the 'water.' It is necessary, then, that the 'bread' of salvation, which nourishes the soul, be 'sent' 'upon the face of' such 'water.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the bread and the waters stand for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The bread is the bread of life, found after the soul is cleansed and found again and again as the days of light multiply.
comments.comment: The bread will be found in the abundance of days. For it will sprinkle the water. Again, to lead toward another meaning, this is said: this bread is not a sensible thing, but it is about that which is said, 'the bread of life has descended from heaven.' This bread must be taken after the cleansing of the soul, as 'he who has desired wisdom has kept the commandments, and the Lord will provide it to him.' First, one receives cleansing—'cleanse your soul, make your soul shining'—and thus one finds the bread 'upon the water,' where 'upon' signifies 'after.' And he says, 'Behold, you find this bread in the abundance of your days.' It does not merely 'work' and nourish for the present, but also 'in the abundance of days.' And this is possible because, as many illuminations come from the 'sun of righteousness,' you have a 'multitude of days' according to 'I will fill them with length of days' and 'he shall be long of life.' 'You will find the bread in the abundance of days.' Even more and more, as it 'shines,' you 'find' the bread of truth, the 'bread of life,' so that the sowing of righteousness was the 'water,' and after the sowing of righteousness, 'upon' the water, you may sow the fruit and the knowledge of the 'light of the true one.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sharing bread may look like throwing it into the water, but over time kindness proves profitable, so one should give unsparingly because the coming day is unknown.
comments.comment: It is right, indeed, to share bread and the other necessities that human beings need for life. For even if for the moment you seem to some to be throwing it away, as though you were handing your bread over to the water (Ecclesiastes 11:1), yet as time goes on your kindness will not prove profitless to you. Give unsparingly, and divide what is yours among many; for you do not know what the coming day will bring about (Ecclesiastes 11:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains casting bread on the waters as giving that seems wasted but proves profitable.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Because we do not know what evil is coming on the earth, we are told to give a portion to the seven and the eight, which means to read the two Scriptures so as to know what to do and what not to do.
comments.comment: For you do not know what will be evil under the earth. … Since you are ignorant of the 'evil upon the earth,' that is, that which is done contrary to the good, or the toil that the 'evil'—that which receives the things men do—has undergone, because of this, do as I command you: 'give a portion to the seven and to the eight'; for from these two scriptures you will 'know' what is being done 'evilly' and what 'evil' is coming against those doing evil. Because of this, 'give a portion to the seven and to the eight.' Moreover, are you then the one 'giving to the seven'? It is not possible otherwise to 'know.' It is as if you say: read then the scripture, for you do not know what you ought to do and what not to do. Because of this, 'know what it is,' what must be done and what must not. Similar to this is 'test all things' (1 Thess 5:21). And why 'test'? So that you may 'retain the good' (1 Thess 5:21) and 'abstain from every form of evil' (1 Thess 5:22).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Clouds filled with rain pour it out on the earth, and in the spiritual sense they are souls ministering the word of salvation, who must be filled with the word before they can rain.
comments.comment:
If the clouds of rain are filled, they pour out upon the earth. And this is according to the spoken truth. When things are well, when those ministered to by providence are well, that is, 'the clouds, having been filled, pour out upon the earth.' Water, if it flows into the sea, is of no use for sowing. Even if all things happening under providence are useful in some other way, they are of no use to the 'earth' if they flow into the Adriatic or into the sea. As for the literal sense, this is so; but this is for the intellect. Souls ministering to the 'word of salvation' happen to be 'clouds being filled with rain.' Moses, being a single 'cloud,' says: 'let my utterance be expected like rain' (Deut 32:2). …

And concerning all who “rain upon” the spiritual “vineyard,” the “house of Israel,” a “command” has been given, when instead of “grapes” it brought forth “thorns,” “not to rain upon it” (Isa 5:2,6). And further in Isaiah itself it is said: “let the clouds sprinkle righteousness, let the earth bring forth mercy” (Isa 45:8). The “sprouting of mercy” comes not from the sensible “earth” but from that which is called the “good earth,” the “good heart,” where the “seed” of Jesus, having fallen, “bore fruit.”

But when are these “clouds” “filled with rain” — that is, with the word — except when “the word of the Lord comes to” them, so that each says: “thus says the Lord to me.” Behold the “rain.” And the “clouds are filled with rain” when “they pour out upon the earth.” If one is not “filled” with the word, he cannot “rain”; nor can he “water” another. Such are the false teachers, who know nothing and suppose they “hold all things.” “Upon the earth” means either humanity or the “heart” of each, prepared for reception: behold, “seed” watered. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of the rain-filled clouds in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The tree that falls stays where it falls, and this speaks of a man, who will be judged as he is found at the end of his life.
comments.comment:
“If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will remain” (Eccl 11:3).

It is clear that this is allegorized and for the anagogy. For who does not know that when someone cuts down “trees,” the “tree” “will remain there, where it falls”? Nor is this true according to the history: for this “tree” is cut not that it “remain there, where it falls,” but that it be carried away for some use. “Tree,” then, here means man. And he says that wherever man is overtaken, “there” he is found and there judged — like “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive according to what he did through the body” (2 Cor 5:10). If “good,” he “falls” to the “south”; if “evil,” to the “north.” …
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the fallen tree signifies and why it is not meant literally.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Every task is to be done in its proper time, so that a man does not reap too early, whether in the field or in his instruction in godliness.
comments.comment:
And seeing in the clouds, he will not reap (Ecclesiastes 11:4). When 'he sees in the clouds,' he sees rain lying upon the earth, 'he will not reap.' We must force the meaning of the word; if a 'rain' is lying upon the crops, the 'rain' being driven down harms the things being reaped, making them moist, and they easily come to rot. This is therefore what the command is: in a suitable 'time' let every 'thing' be done by each one in his own way. Through these two words, he transfers them to all things.

For example, one being introduced into godliness, by way of divine knowledge, let him 'sow' when it is 'time,' receiving lessons which were fitting for the one being introduced to receive. And let him not 'reap' prematurely, but when he sees a 'rain' lying upon the ground capable of watering, then let him 'reap.' For at such times the harvest is taken. The diligent one begins and always has an end in the cutting ahead. The prior labors reach an end, but those following them take up the beginnings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the farmer's rule in the verse and applies it simply.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sower and the reaper can rejoice together, because in the work of the word the beginning is a sowing and the end a reaping.
comments.comment: Such a thing, then, is this, and in the gospel the Savior says concerning the Spirit, of 'reapers' and 'sowers': 'that the sower may rejoice at the same time as the reaper' (John 4:36). But it is not profitable in the same time to 'sow' and 'reap' in the sensible sense. But that of the word, the 'things being reaped' are grown, and those being grown come to 'being reaped.' …  For it has been said, 'when a man has completed, then he begins' (Sirach 18:7); and that which 'begins' and 'completes' happens 'at the same time.' The 'beginning' signifies the 'sowing,' and the 'end' the 'reaping.' 'The sower and the reaper rejoice at the same time.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The works of God are hidden like the forming of a bone in the womb, a thing that those who studied the nature of animals could not explain.
comments.comment: Just as a bone in the belly of a pregnant woman is formed, thus one will not know the 'works' of God. Regarding the incomprehensible of these 'works', it signifies either the hard-to-grasp. Those who have dealt with the nature of animals have spoken of a certain way and a sequence of change for each part; concerning 'bone' they did not have the power to say. … They say that blood is composed in such a way: when food is presented and digested—when it becomes through being sent to be processed—the food changes into blood; and that which is rejected must be cast out, it is not decomposed into the composition of the thing eaten, but is cast off as waste. But when it has been absorbed, then, through a change occurring successively, it is decomposed into blood. Then they say that from the blood, having become thick and congealed, flesh is made, and from the wastes of the food, hair, nails, and such things are made, which are as wastes. But concerning the generation of 'bone', none of them found it, so that this was as 'your judgments are a great abyss' (Psalm 36:6). Such a thing is also what is said in one of the Psalms: 'My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret' (Psalm 139:15). And 'which you made in secret', he says this, that its genesis is hidden; and 'was not hidden' this was 'from you'. Therefore, take this for an illustration. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The works of God stay hidden like a child in the womb until they change into good works, and the strong dogmas are the bones that hold up the passions and the duties.
comments.comment:
Just as 'it is not known' those 'in the womb of the pregnant woman,' unless by chance a revelation from God happens to occur, so the soul, which has attached itself to the seeds and the wombs of the 'bridegroom' of the Savior—about whom it is said, 'he who has the bride is the bridegroom' (John 3:29)—has hidden the wombs. But then they become manifest, when the wombs, which God sowed, change into thought and works. It is not therefore necessary to always have them 'in the womb.' And one has them 'in the womb' and 'bears them' who does not change the words and the thoughts of the works into works and dogmatic contemplations. Just as there 'you do not know' those things, unless they change into good works and pious contemplations, so also one 'will know the works of God' no other way than if they change into works according to energetic operation.

In order that you might receive the strong dogmas as the 'bone of the pregnant woman' by an upward leading; for the 'bones' are the sustaining things of the body. In the same way, without the dogmas of piety, the passions and the duties are not correctly placed. For this reason, it is said concerning these 'bones' that they also have 'knowledge of God' and know that no one is 'like Him.' …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man is told to sow in the morning and not let his hand rest until evening, so that he may gather a good harvest of knowledge from God, since he does not know which seed will succeed.
comments.comment:
… Therefore, you, O man, being exhorted to 'sow in the morning, and let not your hand withhold' (Eccl 11:6) until the 'evening', so that you may receive an excellent 'harvest' of knowledge from God; for 'light your own light of knowledge, and bear fruit unto the fruit of life, until generations of righteousness come to you'.

… Because you do not know what sort of thing will belong, this or that. 'You do not know', he says, 'what this or that will belong to'. If you are 'sowing' but not farming, you do not know whether it bears fruit or does not bear fruit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The same person may sow and reap at once, and the Savior's visit comes as morning to the faithful and as evening to the unfaithful.
comments.comment:
… It is also possible to take this to mean that the same person 'at once' 'sows' and 'reaps', so as not to 'belong' to one kind first and to another kind second 'at once' while all things are happening. And yesterday was a witness to the Gospel that 'so that the sower may rejoice together with the reaper' (John 4:36), as the same 'time' is for both 'seed' and 'harvest'; 'harvest' indeed of the progress already received, and 'seed' of the future to be received.

And the visitation of the Savior may happen to some 'in the morning' and to others 'in the evening'; 'evening' for those who were unfaithful, but 'morning' for those to whom the sun 'has risen' (Ps 118:130) through 'faith' and 'piety'. And this must be said: it is impossible to teach correctly one who has not learned.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sowing at the beginning of instruction lets a man sow again and feed others, as in the blessing of Benjamin, who ate in the morning and gave food in the evening.
comments.comment:
In the very beginning of the introduction to instruction, it is 'sow and let not your hand withhold' so that one might again have a product and 'sow' and feed others. Such a blessing is brought forth in Genesis concerning Benjamin: 'Benjamin', he says, 'a wolf that snatches the morning food and will distribute food in the evening' (Gen 49:27).

The 'wolf that snatches' was when 'he persecuted the church and incited it'; … then indeed 'he ate in the morning', being instructed in the introduction according to faith, 'and in the evening he gave food as nourishment', he became an 'apostle', a 'teacher in faith and truth among the Gentiles'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If a man sows well and reaps well, the two good things come at once, and he has received well both the earlier progress and the later.
comments.comment:
Furthermore, what then is 'you do not know'?—since they are 'at once', you do not have the knowledge that divides this from that. To 'belong' here means to be placed together. … And if the two are the same good things. …

If, he says, 'you sow' well and 'you reap', 'the two good things have happened at once'. And you have received well the preceding progress and have received the following well.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the literal sense the 'day' is one season of sowing and reaping, so a man must sow at its beginning and not slacken, and the harvest stands when the time is fulfilled.
comments.comment:
'In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening let not your hand withhold, for you do not know which this or that will succeed' (Eccl 11:6).

Since we are very much turning toward the literal, and this is to be taken toward history. Often the name of 'day' does not signify only the illuminated air when the sun was above the earth, but also the whole life of man, as if the hymnographer says, 'and I waited for you all the day.' And often 'day' and a 'season' beginning and receiving are called the same. He says therefore that at the beginning of the 'season'—so that you might take the 'day' as one 'season' of 'sowing' and 'reaping'—he says at the beginning of that 'season,' by which there is 'sowing,' do not be slow, 'sow your seed.' …

Your hand finds what it will reap; when the time is fulfilled, the harvest will stand. And these things are spoken in a literal sense.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain, farming sense of the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who sow in tears and into the Spirit sow in the morning of the day, the time after the night of ignorance, so that they may reap eternal life in joy.
comments.comment:
But in an allegorical sense, those 'sowing in tears'—those 'sowing into the Spirit, so that they may reap eternal life'—sow in the beginning of the 'day'; and it is that 'day' which Abraham received with love and longing, so that he might 'see' and be shown by the Savior. And that 'day' is the one of which the choir of the saints says: 'This is the day which the Lord has made'. The apostle also signifies this same thing to the Romans, writing: 'the night is gone, and the day is near, as if we walk decently in the day' (Romans 13:12). Thus he says: the time of 'ignorance' is called 'night'; after this has 'passed', the 'day' succeeds it.

The beginning of the 'day' is 'morning', in which all the saints hasten. One of them says: 'I will stand before you in the morning and watch' (Psalm 5:3), and 'my God, my God, toward you I rise at dawn' (Psalm 63:1). Another says: 'out of the night my spirit rises toward you, O God' (Isaiah 26:9). In this morning, 'sowing in tears', sowing the seeds of virtue with pains, sowing into the Spirit with sweat, so that you may 'reap eternal life', and having 'sown in tears you may reap in joy' (Psalm 126:5) and come 'rejoicing', bringing the sheaves of the seed. Therefore, let not 'your hand' let go of the beginning of the sowing. The word 'sow' applies to both senses.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the morning and the sowing in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The present age is the morning of virtue in which the children of light sow, and the evening belongs to others, since the sun rises for some and sets for others.
comments.comment: It can also be understood thus: since, as 'walking decently in the day', they are both 'children of light' and 'children of the day', these have the 'present age' as the 'morning' of virtue, in which they owe to 'sow', so that in the 'evening' they may 'reap'. Yet that 'evening' is not theirs, but of others; for to them there will be eternal light, the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2) always touching them. You have something similar in a psalm: 'weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning' (Psalm 30:5). The sun 'rises and sets' at once, but not for the same people; to those to whom it 'rises', they 'rejoice'; to those to whom it 'sets', they 'weep'. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Light is insatiable to a healthy eye, for it is 'sweet to the eyes'.
comments.comment: The eye which is healthy and preserves the virtue of sight, when light is present, has a desire for it, and it is never satisfied; for light is insatiable for the eyes: 'sweet to the eyes,' as the Preacher says (Ecclesiastes 11:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man reasons that the sun is fair and life is sweet, that death is fearful, and so advises the young to give their souls to every pleasure.
comments.comment: Someone reasons that the sun is fair (Ecclesiastes 11:7) and this life is sweet, that it is good to live a long time and rejoice all the while (Ecclesiastes 11:8), and that death is fearful, an everlasting evil that brings one to nothing. So he thinks that one ought to enjoy everything that is present and seems pleasant. He also advises the young to make full use of their prime, letting their souls loose into every pleasure, to gratify their desires, to do whatever seems good to them, to look at whatever delights them, and to turn away from whatever does not (Ecclesiastes 11:9).
comments.selected_reason: Shows that Gregory reads 11:7-9 as the voice of a pleasure-seeker, which explains the warning of judgment that follows.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A man who lives many years will be made glad in them if he lives as a true man, keeping the image and likeness of God, and the many years come from the circuit of the sun of righteousness.
comments.comment:
And if a man lives many years, in them... he will be made glad and will remember the days of darkness, because many they will be. … 'Even if a man lives ten thousand years', but he was a 'man' guarding the 'image and likeness' and thus the 'man' has become as 'straight' so as to know the straightness of the light and to 'sow in the morning' and 'not to leave anything to the hand in the evening', 'he will be made glad'. … 'Even if he lives many years, he will be made glad'. And 'many years' come from the cycle of the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2). For just as the perceptible sun, circling a certain circuit, makes 'years' and annual cycles, so also 'the true light'.

Concerning these things, therefore, the holy one who was enlightened by him says: 'I have remembered and meditated on eternal years'. If all things among us are 'temporary', how can 'eternal years' be spoken of as occurring among us? And again: 'I have remembered eternal days, understanding generations of ages'. From 'eternal days' the 'eternal years' are constructed. 'Even if a man lives many years, he will be made glad in them', if he acts thus as a 'man', if he is not 'compared alongside' and becomes 'beast-like', if he is not 'a mare of a horse', 'not wise' according to the 'half-part'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In the literal sense the wise man is glad at all times, even in unpleasant things, and the one who is in virtue remembers the days of darkness and turns away from them.
comments.comment:
Furthermore, the 'even if'? —since not all 'live' these 'years'; but not according to nature does the 'living one live', but if he wills, 'he lives'. If this, therefore, exists, 'he will be made glad' in all the days. Therefore, regarding the literal sense, the truth is not mentioned as such, 'if' someone lives ten thousand 'years', 'he will be made glad in all of them', unless you say it thus: the wise man does not rejoice only over pleasant things, but also over unpleasant things, bravely bearing them; for 'I will bless the Lord' (Ps 34:1).

"At all times," he says, even if the surrounding things were unpleasant and even if they were distressing; just as Job "at all times" "rejoiced" (Job 1:21). And he will remember the days of darkness, because they will be many (Ecclesiastes 11:8). Mostly, the one being in evil does not "remember" the "eternal lights", but the one being in virtue knows even the evil and "remembers" it; thus indeed he "turns away" from it. For until the present they are working, but the wicked are handed over even after these things to the darkness and to other unpleasant things, to all the punishments. The one "remembering", therefore, will not be tried by them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how a man can be glad at all times and still remember the days of darkness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture speaks of forgetting where it means no longer being tried by a thing, as the righteous forget their first affliction when the heaven and the earth are made new.
comments.comment: However, we take "to remember" in a different way; for we also take from the use of memory many times, and the not using of forgetfulness. For when he speaks about the righteous, those enjoying the divine promises, saying "they will forget their first affliction"—instead of saying they will not be tried by it again—"nor will it fall upon their heart again". Why? "For the heaven will be new and the earth will be new"; once my cosmos has been re-measured and the promises have been fulfilled, there will no longer be memory of the distressing. And thus we have become accustomed to say: when a change occurs, we say one takes "forgetfulness of former things", whether they were good or not good. For it is said: "In a good day, the amnesty of evils" (Sirach 11:25). For he does not say this meaning that the one tried by "days of good" and of light realized that he was being tried by "evils". But no longer does he "remember" them according to experience.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What is coming is not eternal, for the things seen are temporary and the unseen are eternal.
comments.comment: "That which is coming" is not eternal; "they are temporary" regarding these "things seen", the visible creatures; but "the unseen" are also "eternal", which the saints strive to possess, saying: "Our aim is not the things seen; for the things seen are temporary, but the unseen are eternal" (2 Cor 4:18). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To let the heart make you good means that virtue of the soul, and not wealth, health or glory, is what makes a man glad.
comments.comment: And let your heart make you good in the days of your youth. 'Let your heart make you good,' not the external things. It has often been said to us regarding the difference between happiness and blessedness, that some place happiness in being fulfilled by the three kinds of goods. Wealth does not 'make good,' it does not truly make one good, nor does health of the body, nor having rank and glory. But possessing virtue of the soul 'rejoices' one. This, therefore, is 'let your heart make you good,' not the external things, not the things concerning the body; do not think greatly upon these, and hasten not to pursue these.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what it means that the heart makes one good.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To walk in blameless paths is to walk the straight paths of virtue and the contemplation of truth, and the word 'walk' shows progress.
comments.comment: And walk in blameless paths. Walk in the 'straight paths' I have spoken of clearly; for the virtues and the activities according to them and the contemplations of the truth are 'good and straight paths.' … Therefore, 'let your heart make you good,' not the accidental things, not the bodily things. Then you will have 'blameless paths' and chance to be blessed; for 'blessed are the blameless in the way' (Ps 119:1) and 'he who walks blamelessly and works righteousness.' And see that 'walking' is not in vain; for it was possible to say both 'stand blameless' and 'sit blameless'; but the walk signifies progress. Therefore, 'walk blameless,' beginning to follow the 'way' with the 'blameless.' Such also is that which is written by Paul: 'we shall walk in newness of life' (Romans 6:4), so that we may progress 'in the newness of life.' Having stripped off the garment of the old life, 'we have put on the new man.' We have a new life, we progress in it, and not turning away from it, we shall not lack.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says to walk and what the blameless paths are.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If the heart is good, the eyes see well, so that a man turns his eye from a prostitute and has an unblemished vision of the eyes.
comments.comment:
And in the vision of your eyes. Take it again in its entirety.

If "your heart is good," you have "eyes" that see well. And in plain words: not seeking foreign beauty, you turn the "eye" away from a prostitute; you do not see a woman for shameful desire, but you have an "unblemished" "vision of the eyes." If you also take the "enlightened eyes of the heart," called the "eyes of the reasoning," the "unblemished" state is much more established.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain, practical sense of the vision of the eyes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God will judge a man in all these things, with punishments for the bad and good things for the earnest, so a man who walks unblemished does not labour in vain.
comments.comment: And know that God will judge you regarding all these things, and remove passion from your heart and drive out evil from your flesh. Do what I command you, knowing "that God will judge you in all these things." "Judgment" measures out punishments for the bad, but promises and good things for the serious. Since you do not destroy in vain, if you "walk" "unblemished in your ways" (Psalm 119:1) and "are rejoiced in the days of your youth" (Ecclesiastes 11:9), strive; for "God will bring you to judgment" regarding these. If they were bad things, for which "judgment" was made toward him, punishment was to be expected; but since they are good—for the "ways" and the divine thoughts are fitting—if you walk thus "unblemished," you do not destroy in vain; for "God leads you in these to judgment."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man who advises pleasure is out of his senses, for he does not expect God's judgment, and senselessness leads to ruin.
comments.comment: To him [the man who urges pleasure] I will say only this: You there, you are out of your senses, for you do not expect the judgment that will come from God for all these things (Ecclesiastes 11:9). Profligacy and licentiousness are evil, and the filthy abuse of our bodies is deadly (Ecclesiastes 11:10). For senselessness follows close on youth, and senselessness leads to ruin (Ecclesiastes 11:10).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain answer to the call to pleasure, with the reason.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The passionate part is joined to the heart and the lustful part to the flesh.
comments.comment: And turn away anger from your heart and lead away evil from your flesh. From here we know that the passionate part is joined to the heart, and the lustful part to the flesh. Now he says evil: the fornication and the gluttony.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Passion is not a virtue of the heart but of the spirited part, so it is to be restrained there and not mixed with the mind, which the name 'heart' signifies.
comments.comment:
And remove passion from your heart. "Passion" is not a virtue of the "heart," but of the spirited part. Therefore he says: do not use your reasoning and your mind for "passion," but, even if this movement ever stands in the spirited part, restrain it in your "heart." Thus it is removed "from your heart," not by being mixed with it.

The soul is tripartite, as many have said. And the matter is such: we have various senses. Just as it is not possible to see by hearing, nor to touch or smell by intellect, so we appear to have the inner man and the soul itself. We have a spirited power, a reasoning power, and a desiring power. From where do we know this? Observe that the reasoning is distinct from the spirited and the desiring from the irrational animals: irrational animals have a spirited power and "passion," and a desiring power and desire, but they do not have reasoning. Since they do not have reasoning, it is evident they do not have the reasoning part, they do not have mind. And the mind is signified by the name of the "heart."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Anger must not be led into the heart, where it would become a settled disposition, and when anger leaves the heart the evil deeds done through the body pass away too.
comments.comment: He continues in the Scripture. Therefore he says that, even if you should ever be angry, do not lead the 'anger' into the 'heart', so that the 'anger' does not become a disposition. And if you should have a desire having suddenly become in the desiring part, do not carry it into the mind and the reasoning faculty; for it will be a disposition and no longer a passion or a pre-passion, but wickedness. And lead away evil from your flesh: 'And from your flesh lead away the evil' (Ecclesiastes 11:10). And unbridledness seems to be a wickedness of desire; therefore 'lead it away from your flesh'. And it is possible also thus: if 'the anger departs from your heart', you do not practice evil through the members and the body; the one being angry strikes many times and threatens and intends to murder. When therefore 'the anger departs from your heart', those things happening through actions which are evil also pass away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is meant by removing anger from the heart and evil from the flesh.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Youth is open to folly, so the young man is told to rejoice and to walk blamelessly, so that he may not have folly, vanity or evil of the flesh.
comments.comment: If the young man does not 'walk' 'in the ways blameless', nor does he do the other things which he was appointed to do, he is in 'ignorance'. It is also said in proverbs by this wise man: 'Folly spreads from the heart of a youth' (Proverbs 22:15). 'Ignorance' is disguised by 'youth'. If indeed anyone exceeds the movement of 'youth' and moves like an old man as if in 'youth', he has much 'ignorance'. 'That I may give cunning to the innocent, and perception and understanding to the young child'. If 'perception and understanding are given to the young child' by wisdom, it is evident that he has cast away 'ignorance'. When he does not have knowledge, he is in thoughtlessness. For this reason also in the Psalms such things were joined to 'youth': 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Ps 25:7). See that 'youth' is most receptive to these things and possesses them. Therefore 'rejoice', so that you may not have 'folly'; therefore 'walk', so that you may not have 'vanity' and 'evil of the flesh'. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God created you in your youth so that you might take up knowledge, not so that you might have ignorance, and when you possess virtue vice has no place in you.
comments.comment:
… therefore, in the day of your youth, remember who created you. God is the one who 'created' Eccl 12:1; it is not that God 'creates' vices in me. For this reason, observe that He 'created you in youth,' not so that you might have 'ignorance,' not so that you might be thoughtless, not so that you might be unlearned, but so that, being receptive to knowledge, you might take it up.

Until the days of your vice arrive Eccl 12:1. If he means by 'vice' this thing which is contrary to virtue and brings boastfulness to the one possessing it, he says: 'until the days of your vice do not come,' meaning as long as you are receptive to virtue and 'vice'—do not expect 'vice,' and do not prepare yourself for it. For when you possess virtue, 'vice' has no place in you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what remembering the Creator in youth means in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God does not bring punishment by chance but when He judges it beneficial, being long-suffering, so one should repent before the coming evil arrives.
comments.comment:
Regarding punishment, the 'evil' that is coming, do what I tell you, so that the coming punitive evil may not find you liable. Does punishment come before? God brings punishment upon men not as it happens by chance, but when He judges it beneficial to bring it upon them; for the Lord is a 'righteous judge, powerful and long-suffering, not bringing wrath on every single day; if they do not turn back, He will whet His sword' (Ps 7:11). Since God is a 'righteous judge,' how is it that sinning men do not fall under punishment and retribution? Is it because, through weakness, He 'did not bring it'? No; He is 'powerful' and was able to punish immediately, but with His power He is also 'long-suffering' and 'does not bring wrath on every single day'; for those whom He 'brings wrath upon' and those whom He does not, He knows through His most profound words. Therefore, when they despise the warning of the threat because the 'evil' has been hidden, as if it were necessary only to be punished later, then 'if they do not turn back' to whom He was long-suffering, 'He will whet His sword.'

This is the 'evil' that is 'coming,' being not a habit in the hand, but a punitive, most violent affliction. In the 'time' therefore of 'judgment,' upon every 'time,' He judges all. And He calls this 'time' at once a 'time of judgment' and at once a 'day of wrath' and a 'day of retribution.' 'Until this evil comes,' 'until the evil has come,' repent. 'Repentance' has a 'place'; 'the Lord of the promise is not slow, as some think He is slow, but is long-suffering toward them, not wishing to destroy anyone, but wishing to bring all to repentance' (2 Pet 3:9). Since therefore 'repentance' is given to you as a superior thing, repent before the 'evil comes.'
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms why one should repent now: God is patient but will judge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: One must fear God while young, before the day when the sun, moon and stars shine no more and the guardian angels are shaken.
comments.comment: One must fear God while still young (Ecclesiastes 12:1), before giving oneself over to evils, before the great and terrible day of God comes, when the sun will shine no more, nor the moon, nor the rest of the stars (Ecclesiastes 12:2; Matthew 24:29), and the higher powers, the angels who guard the world, will be shaken in that storm and turmoil of all things (Ecclesiastes 12:3).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the darkened sun and the trembling keepers as the day of God and the angels who guard the world.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The sun of righteousness is darkened not by being put out but by becoming distant from those no longer worthy to be illumined by it, as the sun seems darkened to us at night.
comments.comment: 'Until the sun is darkened'; and it is possible to take it thus: as much as we in this life have our present existence unhindered, we are able to be illumined by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2) and by the 'light of the true one' and by the 'moon and the stars.' But we take the 'moon' more allegorically as the ecclesiastical opinion; and toward the 'sun of righteousness,' 'moon' may be said to be the teaching which is able to enlighten there. And likewise, the 'stars' are taken as the ministers of the divine gift, the 'angels,' in whom God 'speaks' His 'word.' They are 'darkened,' therefore, that is, from you; for the 'sun' is by no means extinguished at once. And just as in the nights it seems to us that the 'sun' itself is 'being darkened,' not because it suffers, but because it is becoming distant from us, far from our sight, so also the 'sun of righteousness' 'is being darkened' to those who are no longer worthy of being illumined by it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the darkening of the sun can be understood as light withdrawn from the unworthy.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The clouds are those ministering the spiritual rain, men or angels, who turn back when rain would not benefit.
comments.comment: And they shall turn the clouds back behind the rain. 'Clouds' have often been said to be those ministering the spiritual 'rain,' namely men or angels. And these 'turn back' 'behind the rain,' no longer ministering the 'rain'; for it is not advantageous then for the 'rain' to come.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Earth that holds the seeds of thorns is better not watered, so the clouds, men or angels, no longer minister the rain to it, but pour it on approved earth.
comments.comment:
Take up virtue and stand apart from evil; and he says: “For the earth which drinks in the rain that often comes upon it, and brings forth vegetation useful to those for whom it is cultivated, receives blessing from God; but bearing thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to cursing, its end” (Heb 6:7-8); and after other things he says: “but we are persuaded of better things concerning you, beloved, things that belong to salvation” (Heb 6:9) — instead of: having duly used the “rain” and been watered, you bore what he called “the vegetation of salvation.”

They no longer minister the “rain” to you — for this does not happen to you advantageously; you have the seeds of “thorns and thistles” laid up within. It is advantageous, then, for “earth” so disposed not to be watered, lest sprouting occur of the evils laid up within and the passions change into vices and dispositions. If, then, we are so as to be “approved earth” and “bringing forth useful vegetation,” the “clouds” pour the “rain” that increases the spiritual “vegetations.” Again: the ministering angels? — “Are they not all ministering spirits sent forth for service for those who are about to inherit salvation?” (Heb 1:14). And men too minister the divine “rain,” and to these it is commanded to “sprinkle righteousness” (Isa 45:8), not to “sprinkle” water, not to pour rain.
comments.selected_reason: Uses an easy image of rain on good and thorny ground to explain why the clouds turn back.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Scripture uses "house" for several things, such as a person's conduct and manner of life, and often for the place around the earth.
comments.comment: “In the day when the guards of the house are shaken” (Eccl 12:3). The name “house” is used in the inspired Scriptures for various things. For when he says that the one who “heard” the “words” of Jesus and changed them into deeds “builds his own house upon the rock” (Matt 7:24), he calls the conduct and the practical and contemplative life the “house” of the doer. And “the houses of transgressors shall owe cleansing, but the houses of the just are acceptable” calls lives and conducts “houses.” And “since the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves” (Exod 1:21) — “having feared” him, they had both fear and “house” and “stronghold”: for “the fear of the Lord is a stronghold of the holy” (Prov 14:26). And by the name “house” is often signified the place around the earth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the "house" of the verse can mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Vessels of gold are those who purify the mind, vessels of silver those who minister the word, and wood and clay are dishonorable, yet one who purifies himself becomes a vessel for honor.
comments.comment:
Thus he says: in the world there are diligent men; and these are 'vessels' of 'gold and silver' (2 Timothy 2:20).

And whoever 'purifies' their own mind and works through fire, they are 'gold vessels', having diligence concerning the intelligible things, being moved toward the supra-cosmic things. But 'silver' vessels are those ministering the word. For it has often been demonstrated that the 'word' stands for the name of 'silver'. …

Others are 'silver', being able by word to make clear what has been perceived to them and what they read. And there are other 'vessels of wood and clay'. And of these, 'some for honor, others for dishonor' there are (2 Timothy 2:20). The 'gold and silver' are precious, but the 'wood and clay' are 'dishonorable'. The 'wood' is able to be consumed by fire, and the 'clay' is such as it is 'to be crushed'.

But natures are not introduced here as unchangeable, as the myth of the heterodox desires. For it follows that 'if anyone purifies himself from the dishonor of them', it is evident that 'as a vessel', 'he will be a vessel for honor to the master for every good work'; so that by himself someone becomes a dishonorable and ignoble 'vessel'.

There is indeed a transition occurring from the honorable to the dishonorable; for it has been said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah regarding a great change having happened to Israel from piety to impiety and from practical virtue to practical wickedness: 'the precious sons of Zion, adorned with gold' and silver, 'how they were counted as vessels of clay' (Lamentations 4:2). You see that the precious things are made of gold and silver.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The "house" may be the church, which has vessels for honor and dishonor, and its guards, the teachers attended by angels, abandon those whose evil has grown.
comments.comment:
Therefore: here does he say "house" for the world or the church? For in this too there are such diverse "vessels" "for honor and for dishonor". And that such things are in the church, the divine word says: "remove the evil one from among yourselves" (1 Corinthians 5:13), "vessels of dishonor" etc. Again, "fornication is heard among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, that a man has a woman of his father" (1 Corinthians 5:1). And he commands "to cast out" this one. And the church can be the "great house" and the surrounding place. And "guards" of this "house" are those appointed to watch.

If you take the church, the teachers — and angels attend upon these. Concerning Peter, at any rate, they said: “It is his angel” (Acts 12:15). And the little ones in the church have angels “always beholding the face of the Father” (Matt 18:10); and if the little ones, how much more the perfect. Again: if these are “shaken”? — the evil of those being guarded has intensified: the guards will abandon them, whether they were perfect men or angels. For they say: “Come, let us abandon her” — as the Holy Spirit cries out beforehand, saying: “The daughter of Zion shall be abandoned like a tent in a vineyard” (Isa 1:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The guards of the house are shaken when its sentries leave, as when Josephus tells of a voice in the temple saying "We are departing from here" and as when the Savior said "I have forsaken my house".
comments.comment:
There was a Jewish historian, Josephus. In the divine portents that happened after the Savior was betrayed by the Jews, he set down this one too, which he relates: there was a great door of the temple; thirty strong men could scarcely shut it, and bars were laid on that it might be secured when shut. Suddenly, he says, in one night the priests going their rounds heard, he says, a voice as of many saying: “We are departing from here”; and suddenly, he says, the gates opened of themselves. And this was the “daughter of Zion shall be abandoned like a tent in a vineyard.”

And this happened most of all when the Savior “abandoned,” saying: “I have forsaken my house, I have left my heritage” (Jer 12:7); “behold, your house is left to you,” the Savior says again to the Jews themselves. This, then, is the “guards of the house being shaken”: the sentries being removed, no longer tending the “house.”
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The men of power are the rulers, and their perversion is their removal from the rule entrusted to them.
comments.comment: “And the men of power are perverted; and the grinding women have ceased, because they have grown few; and those that look through the windows are darkened” (Eccl 12:3). The “men of power” are these: those who rule the house as generals — the rulers. “Perversion” does not mean their wickedness, but the transfer from the rule with which they had been entrusted.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what the "men of power" and their "perversion" mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those looking in the eye-sockets are the souls using the senses, or those who search the Scriptures and are enlightened.
comments.comment:
And those 'looking in the eye-sockets' will darken. These 'looking in the eye-sockets' are the souls using the senses. For the senses are to be taken as 'eye-sockets'. Therefore, those 'looking in the eye-sockets' will 'darken'. …

It is also possible to take it this way: those 'searching the Scriptures' and 'paying attention to the reading' of them find 'eye-sockets', through which they are able to be enlightened, and the light that exists within.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: On that day men of power and women at their work will cease and hide with the doors shut, and the lawless will be flung away like a worthless caper bush.
comments.comment: So men of power will cease, and the women at their work will cease too (Ecclesiastes 12:3), fleeing into the dark corners of the houses with all the doors shut (Ecclesiastes 12:4). A woman who has stopped grinding for fear will speak in the faintest voice, like the smallest bird (Ecclesiastes 12:4). All the impure women will fall to the ground (Ecclesiastes 12:4), and so will cities and their bloodstained governments, as they await the punishment from above, when a most bitter and bloody season has set in, like an almond tree in flower, when punishments press on without pause, like a swarm of locusts flying down, and when the lawless are flung out of the way like a black and worthless caper bush (Ecclesiastes 12:5).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the images of these verses as the terrors of the day of judgment.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The marketplace is the church, and its doors are shut after this life, when teaching is no longer present in the time of judgment.
comments.comment: And they will shut doors in the marketplace in the weakness of the voice of the truth. … I spoke concerning human matters, those 'being seen and being timely'. Concerning the coming age and the end of the present age he teaches and says that 'they will shut doors in the marketplace' (Ecclesiastes 12:4). And 'marketplace' here he means the church, as the rhetoricians say. As long as this life exists, the 'marketplaces' or the 'marketplace', the church, exist, in which those who speak are speaking. But 'it will be shut' after these things, when teaching is no longer present in the 'time of judgment'. I do not say this to mean that there will not be instruction in the ages to come, but according to that 'time' in which those being judged 'stand at the judgment seat of Christ' (Romans 14:10); for they have a word regarding what has been done, regarding being instructed or being taught.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the shut doors of the marketplace mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those closing the marketplace are the teachers, who shut the doors when they no longer have hearers to teach, so as not to give the holy thing to dogs or cast pearls before swine.
comments.comment:
It must be said, because of the truth, what is the inherent nature of things. What then are those 'closing the marketplace'? They are the teachers. This is similar to what is said in Isaiah, though rather according to a different thought than the literal words: 'I am being finished by the clouds so that no rain falls upon it'; for from receiving the 'rain', they were turning the 'thorns' and the 'thistles' into plants, but the intention of the 'clouds' and what was commanded to them was that the 'vineyard might bring forth brief grapes'; but since instead of 'grapes' they had grown 'thorns', not wishing to increase the evil again by stinginess, He 'commanded' them 'not to rain'.

In this way also these teachers, since they no longer had those whom they ought to teach, 'closed the doors in the marketplaces'. And this happens in this way many times, for when the teachers hear: 'Do not give the holy thing to the dogs, nor cast pearls before the swine, lest turning they throw them upon you and trample you' (Matt 7:6). Toward this, again, 'it is not given to those'. For they were about to be more impious, 'trampling' the divine words which are the 'pearls', and decorating the 'inner man' with worldly things; not even observing the beauty or the preciousness of them, they were about to 'trample' them instead of regarding them highly. So in a certain way they 'close the doors in the marketplace' here; and if so here, much more there, until the judgment seat and the tribunal be 'opened'.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who shuts the doors and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sparrow may be the Savior, who said "I became as a sparrow upon a roof", or the proclamation of the truth, which cries out above to the perfect hearers.
comments.comment:
'And the daughters of song shall rise up to the voice of a sparrow, and all the daughters of song shall be humbled' (Ecclesiastes 12:4). The 'marketplace' will 'rise up to the voice of a sparrow'. Those 'knowing in part and prophesying' 'closed' the 'marketplace' and its 'doors'. These are the 'apostles', the 'prophets', the 'teachers' among men. Let us show that even the spiritual beings 'sent for ministry' are 'withdrawn' 'to the voice of a sparrow'. A 'sparrow' may be said to be the Savior here according to the man, according to: 'And I became as a sparrow upon a roof' (Psalm 102:7). And each of the birds, when 'having heard the words' of Jesus, turns them into works and 'builds a house' and fills the building and crowns the building, cries out 'upon the roof' in vigilance.

As if raising the 'voice'. The proclamation of the truth can also be called a 'sparrow' then, becoming lofty, since it once happened below for the hearers. But since now even the perfect hearers have become inspired and pursue the things above, there the 'sparrow upon the roof' cries out to them; the perfect has cried out, happening above the world, to face 'face to face' with the truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The proclamation of the resurrection is called a sparrow, as it is compared to a trumpet, and those who rise are raised incorruptible, strong and spiritual.
comments.comment:
'Rising to the voice of the sparrow', since it is also possible for them themselves to 'rise' concerning which the word speaks according to the expected resurrection. The proclamation of the resurrection signifies one thing in many ways. For when it is compared to a 'trumpet'—'the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall rise incorruptible' (1 Cor 15:52)—this trumpeter is the herald of the resurrection, calling so that all having heard the summons may 'rise'. For this reason it is compared to a 'trumpet'. And this instrument is loud-voiced and is heard everywhere. Thus also here the proclamation of the resurrection said 'sparrow', which seems not to be undignified.

The 'rising ones' are 'being raised', but instead of 'corruptible' they are 'incorruptible', instead of 'dishonorable' and 'weak' they are 'strong' and 'glorious', instead of 'psychic' they are 'spiritual'. Therefore, there will be a 'rising into the voice of the sparrow'. But how will that 'marketplace' which was 'closed' 'rise'? It will 'rise' in the whole world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the rising at the voice as the resurrection of the dead.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who took no oil found no sellers when it was too late, since it was no longer a place of instruction, and the doors of the marketplace are not open when many oppose the word.
comments.comment:
The five who have gathered oil, pressed from the true olive tree, possessing that which provides nourishment and illuminates, entered with the bridegroom into the banquet when a cry occurred in the middle of the night: 'The bridegroom comes, go out to meet him' (Matt 25:6). But those who did not take oil in the vessels, having neglected the one who guards the light, went out to buy and no longer found those selling them; for it was no longer a place of instruction then, nor were those selling the divine words present. And because of this, they remained outside.

And here, therefore, when the village is gathered, the 'marketplaces' are 'closed'; they do not have those 'open doors' about which the divine words write. For indeed the apostle says: 'A great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many who oppose me' (1 Cor 16:9). If the 'great door' of the word is 'opened' and 'effective', then 'many who oppose' are present. And it is 'effective' when those who hear convert the teachings into works. And 'many' become 'opposing'; for if we observe the Scriptures, it is not always that false prophets are found when they are prophets, nor are false apostles present at other times when they are apostles and teachers. For, envying, they 'oppose' and attempt to contradict the truth, attempting to contradict those who teach well, sometimes even attacking them and leading them to death. Therefore, a 'door' 'has been opened to me, great and effective'. It is not that the 'marketplace' was 'shut', but the 'doors' of the 'marketplace' were not 'open'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The doors of wisdom are the doors of the marketplace, and they are closed when the place of instruction is gathered, voluntarily and not by force.
comments.comment: And in another epistle of his he says: 'After I had come and a door had been opened, I had no respite for my spirit, not finding Titus my brother' (2 Corinthians 2:12). Before the 'door was opened', he 'had no respite' so as to bring forward the word without finding those who cooperate with him. And in the proverbs it is said: 'Blessed is the man who listens to me, and the man who, if he keeps my ways, remains watchful at my doors by day' (Prov 8:34). The 'doors' of wisdom are the 'doors' of the 'marketplace'. Therefore the 'doors' in the 'marketplace' are 'closed' when the place of instruction is gathered. And see that they 'close' the 'doors' voluntarily. The 'closing' of the 'doors' is not by force.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The voice of the grinding woman, a holy soul or church, is weak and does not speak so boldly when hearers do not benefit, as Moses' defense seemed an accusation to those who did not believe.
comments.comment:
But when the “doors” of the “marketplace” have been “shut,” consider what happens “in the weakness of the voice of the grinding woman” (Eccl 12:4). We were told that there is a “grinding woman taken up” — grinding well and making “flour” and “fine flour” useful — and another “abandoned,” having “sown wind-spoiled things”; and she has “flour” from which it is not possible to make bread. The “one,” then, the “taken up,” has its “voice” “in weakness.” But I want to say something newer, which I am eager not to have trampled down.

“In weakness,” he says, “is the voice of the grinding woman” — of the “taken up,” not of the “abandoned.” But it does not admit speechlessness entirely: for it is a holy soul or a holy church; and after these things too, as is possible, it speaks. But the paradox, which I said I would speak, is this: we once said concerning Moses that he did not speak against the Jews with the intention of an accuser. For the Savior said this: “Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father; Moses is the one accusing you, in whom you have hoped. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; but if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5:45-47).

He did not “accuse,” then, with the intention of speaking against them — since even concerning those who “made the calf” he interceded, saying: “If you forgive them their sin, forgive; but if not, blot me too out of your book which you wrote” (Exod 32:32). Thus, then, he “accused.” Since they “did not believe” even “his writings,” he defends himself, saying: “I kept silent about nothing of what was revealed to me; but when God said: ‘Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and tell the sons of Israel’ (Exod 19:3), I spoke, and there is nothing of what was revealed that I kept silent about.” The defense, then, which he spoke, seemed to be an accusation of them, since when he spoke the things leading to faith and proof, they did not receive them. So too here “weak” is the “voice of the grinding woman.” She does not speak so boldly as when the hearers benefit and those nourished by the “grinding women,” but in a way she defends herself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The daughters of song are false teachers, daughters of voice alone and not of mind, wisdom or light, and their nothingness is exposed as darkness is dissolved by light.
comments.comment: The false teachers are “daughters” of “song”; they are “daughters” of “voice” alone, not of mind, nor of wisdom, nor of knowledge, nor of light. And because of their unintelligible and because of what has been exposed concerning the “pro kairos,” these “daughters” are spoken of.
