Therefore these “shall be humbled”; and in the way that darkness is dissolved by the presence of light, so by the presence of “rising to the voice of a sparrow,” or the “marketplace,” or the Savior, or the divine teachers, their nothingness is exposed. It is shown that their teaching had existence only insofar as it lived by the presence of the moment … Furthermore, do we have something to say from another scripture appropriately? “Turn away from me the sound of your songs, and the melody of your psalter I shall not hear” (Amos 5:23); their “song” is considered a disturbance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the daughters of song are humbled: their teaching lived only by the voice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever sees from on high, with a high heart and mind, sees that the ways hold amazements.
comments.comment: 'And from on high they shall see and be amazed in the way; and the almond shall blossom, and the thorn shall grow thick' (Ecclesiastes 12:5). If anyone sees from on high, being called high, having a high heart and a high mind, he sees that 'in the ways there are amazements' (Ecclesiastes 12:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whatever is proclaimed as near confounds the mind, as men fear lightning and thunder, and so the loud-voiced divine word, which is called thunder, produces amazement.
comments.comment: In general, the things proclaimed about the use confound the mind concerning such things; and especially when it is believed to be near, it confounds the mind and “amazement” results. They are amazed at the things said, and just as in sensible things, if a lightning strike is expected, all fear; when thunder comes, all are afraid. The psalmist said this too: “at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid” (Psalm 104:7; LXX 103:7). And just as from the sensible “voice” they take fear, being confounded, so from the loud-voiced divine word, about which it is said as of “thunder”: “the God of glory thundered” (Psalm 29:3; LXX 28:3) and again “the Lord thundered from heaven” (2 Sam 22:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The almond puts out leaves before all other plants in spring and lasts, which is why the priestly rod was of almond-wood, and it blossomed before the others.
comments.comment:
“And the almond shall blossom” (Eccl 12:5). Those who have spoken about the nature of plants say this about the “almond”: before all plants in spring it puts forth leaves and casts them off after the casting-off of all the other trees; it is lasting, then. For this reason the priestly “rod” was said to be of “almond-wood” (Numbers 17:8). For it did not remain for a few days: from Moses until the visitation of the Savior it appeared.

They were deacons of these traditions. And they quickly 'flourished' and quickly withered. But the priestly 'rod' of 'almond-wood,' being so, remained for long, until a succession might be born from the greater and more spiritual priesthood; and it blossomed before the others.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A true teaching and a false one arise together, and the almond blossoms when the false teachings are humbled, for the greatness of the truth is shown most when there is great falsehood for it to overcome.
comments.comment:
And this must be said: that there will be a true teaching and a false and deceptive one. For they say: in the times of the prophets, false prophets are found; for the evil is a mimic of the true. From the time that Christ appeared in visitation, many false Christs promised to come.

We say therefore this: even if those of the other teachings were plants, and later 'blossom' after the upright teaching and before it; for when it appears, they are quenched. This 'rod' therefore loosed the 'rods' of the others, of the false apostles, of the false prophets. Will the 'almond' therefore 'blossom'?—this: when 'the daughters of the song are humbled' (Song of Solomon), the promised false teachings, false 'rods', then even more 'the almond will blossom'.

Regarding the apostolic word, we say that there will be a standing of righteousness when injustice prevails among men. Loosing the injustice and revealing those who advocate it, being something great, its greatness would not have been shown if there were not a great injustice which it loosed. And we say that 'the truth of God prevailed in human falsehood'. And we say that then, especially, the good appeared of the truth, when many false sophists came into the midst, promising contentious words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The almond has a bitter husk, a shell and an edible kernel, like the body, soul and spirit, and it blossoms when the whole man is sanctified and his body transformed like Christ's.
comments.comment: The 'almond' has two perimeters outside the edible part: shell-like and then bitter, the husk which is on the outside. The outside husk may be the body; for it is bitter, having a relation to pleasure. But that shell-like husk is the soul, for it is well-proportioned and large; and within is the edible, the spirit. When therefore that thing of the time of the apostle writing is fulfilled: 'May the God of peace sanctify you wholly, your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23), 'the almond has blossomed'; for in the 'blossoming' these three things are contained. Therefore the man 'blossoms' when he advances in virtue, having 'the body being transformed' (Philippians 3:21) so as to become 'conformed' to the 'body' of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the blossoming almond with an image a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man goes into the house of his age, the life after this one, when the fleeting and trivial things are loosed and he departs into the place of incorruption.
comments.comment:
And the caparis might be scattered, because the man went into the house of his age. The 'house of the age' of the 'man' is the life after these things. All the things spoken are happening: and 'the doors are shut in the marketplace', and 'they rise up to the voice of the sparrow' (Ecclesiastes 12:4) those being called to this, and 'the daughters of the singer are humbled' (Ecclesiastes 12:4). Those who are in the 'house' of the 'age' are the 'men'. And the place concerning the earth is the 'house' of this 'age of the evil one'. All the things spoken are happening. Since therefore he 'went into' another 'age', he went 'into' the age of 'his own house', 'into' that after these things.

All things having passed away here are loosed. It is possible to take it this way also, since the 'man' is according to the soul. When all the things that have come to him are loosed—the fleeting things, the trivial things—he 'goes into' his own remaining 'house,' having left this 'age.' And an 'age' is appropriate and a 'house' is for the 'man' who has become a divine state, being 'according to the image and likeness of God,' from which he 'departed' from this 'age.' Those things are loosed, as if someone says that fornication has ceased. For the 'man departed into' the place of incorruption.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speakers in the marketplace lament as at a dirge, as in the children's cry "We played the flute for you and you did not dance", and those who cut their breasts raise up feeling in themselves.
comments.comment: And those being cut in mourning surrounded him in the marketplace (Matt 12:5). Therefore, 'after the flute has been played' and 'the wailing' is increasing, those formerly speaking in the marketplace, as if lamenting them, speak. Therefore, 'in the marketplace those being cut surrounded him.' You also have it said in the Gospel by the Savior: 'To what generation shall I liken this generation?' and he says: 'It is like children sitting in the marketplace, calling to one another: We played the flute for you and you did not dance; we mourned for you and you did not weep' (Matt 11:17). And he adds: 'John came neither eating nor drinking' (Matthew 11:18). Behold the 'lamenting of the child'; for John is taken for all the ancient Scripture and those who ministered to it, but the Son of Man is taken for the body of the Church, the apostolic and evangelical choir. He says, therefore, that the 'children play the flute,' so it is necessary for those hearing the flute to 'dance.' But the 'dancing' of the imitation of words is promised to be made through the hands. When, therefore, they hear the word of the wise of salvation and the word bringing forth piety, and are conformed to the announced works and the intellect, they 'dance' praiseworthily according to the dancing which David 'danced' before the ark (2 Sam 6:14). For when they 'lament' calling to repentance, raising up feeling, they 'cut their breasts,' because this raises up feeling. When one laments and cuts his breast because another is sinning, he immediately says, 'How much this one reproaches himself for my sake, I also ought to do this.' And these, therefore, hearing the lament, if they 'cut their breasts' bearing their hands against their chests, they raise up feeling for themselves.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The teachers rejoice when the hearers are set straight and are grieved when the divine decrees are heard against them, and the church is a marketplace, as the Greeks use the word.
comments.comment: The teachers rejoice when the hearers are being made straight; they are grieved when the divine decrees are heard against them. Since, therefore, even after the hearers sin, the teachers pity them in proclaiming the divine, 'those being cut cry out', … And the New Testament knows the church as a 'marketplace', just as the Greeks do. In the Acts of the Apostles, indeed, it says that 'they have' certain requests, 'market-people lead them', that is to say, rhetoricians. 'You are able', he says, 'to move a case concerning this, those who are proclaiming, the rhetoricians'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The good man goes rejoicing to his eternal home, while the wicked beat their breasts and find that stored silver and gold are of no use any longer.
comments.comment: The good man will go rejoicing to his own eternal home; but the wicked will fill all that is theirs with beating of breasts (Ecclesiastes 12:5), and neither silver laid up in store nor tested gold will be of use any longer (Ecclesiastes 12:6). For a great blow will seize everything, even down to the jar standing at a spring, and the wheel of a carriage that happens to have been left in the hollow (Ecclesiastes 12:6), …
comments.selected_reason: Reads the long home as the good man's eternal home and the silver and gold as stored wealth that no longer helps.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The silver cord is the word of the Lord, whose cords are woven from fitting sayings, and as long as it is active those in the marketplace surround and lament the disobedient.
comments.comment: Toward a literal sense: 'the silver cord' may be the giving and the receiving concerning transactions. Toward a spiritual sense: since the word of the Lord is 'silver' and 'his words are refined silver', 'cords' are woven from these; … “Gold,” then, must be taken here as the mind; and “silver” as the uttered word. “Gold” you take here as the meaning, and “flower-ornament” as the ruling part, as being the case and guard of the “gold.” And if “silver” signifies the word and the scripture of God, it is a weaving to take fitting sayings with fitting ones, and to join the understanding of these to those and of those to these. Again: does he not mean the church by “until”? — he means this: “in the marketplace those being cut are cut as they surround.” “Marketplace” is the ecclesiastical teaching. And by ecclesiastical I do not mean altogether that of the Christians, but the congregational. This, then, is what he says: that as long as the “silver cord” “is active,” they “surround” and “lament” the disobedient.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the silver cord is overturned, lamentation will no longer accomplish anything, though the writer does not say there will never be repentance.
comments.comment: But when it “is overturned,” “when that which is in part is abolished” (1 Cor 13:10), no longer do “those being cut surround the marketplace”; for their lamentation will no longer effect anything then, when each hears: “now you repent, when there is no ‘time.’” But I do not say this, that there will never be repentance, but then, when the “time of judgment” is active, when “they stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive what he did through the body” (2 Cor 5:10). Again: but if it “is not overturned”? — this: then “those being cut surround in the marketplace,” while the word of the teaching is still “active,” though they are not persuaded, not assenting, not bound by the “silver cord”; for the one who assents is bound.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The presence abolishes the partial: we crush lesser things into greater, as on seeing one we had only heard.
comments.comment: [Of the golden ornament that is "crushed":] And what is the 'face to face'? We often encounter this, where the presence 'abolishes the partial'. Often we say that something is more pleasant for one to hear, from which we would be benefited if we see him; there we 'crush' those things, because we perceive greater things, we 'cast out' them; we do not set them aside, but rather we 'crush' them into greater things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wheel draws water from a pit, and when no longer needed it runs upon the pit and destroys it.
comments.comment: It is possible to draw from a parallel 'pit'; just as it is to draw 'water' from a 'spring', so also to draw water from a 'pit' with a 'wheel'. When therefore there is no longer a need to move it thus, then 'the wheel shall run upon the pit' and destroys it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Souls are saved by knowing their begetter and flying up to Him.
comments.comment: For human beings who lie upon the earth there is one salvation: that their souls come to know Him by whom they were begotten, and fly up to Him (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
comments.selected_reason: Says what the spirit's return to God means: the soul comes to know its begetter and flies up to Him.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The preacher repeats that human things are utterly empty, laments that his hearers cannot be taught, and says that in old age he has labored to find what pleases God.
comments.comment: So I say again what I have said before: human beings are in a state of utter emptiness, and the emptiness of the things they devise could not be greater (Ecclesiastes 12:8). My labor is wasted as I preach wisely to the assembly, since I am trying to teach this people, who are unteachable and past cure (Ecclesiastes 12:9). It takes a man of noble spirit to be able to understand words of wisdom. Now that I am old and have passed through a long span of life, I have labored to find out what is pleasing to God through the mysteries of the truth (Ecclesiastes 12:10).
comments.selected_reason: Gives the Preacher's closing words on vanity and on his own search for what pleases God.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: The precepts of the wise rouse souls like an ox goad, and teachers hand them on from one good Shepherd and Teacher.
comments.comment: I know that the precepts of the wise rouse souls and prick them no less than bodies are stirred when pierced by an ox goad or a nail (Ecclesiastes 12:11). Some will hand on those wise teachings, having received them from one good Shepherd and Teacher (Ecclesiastes 12:11); all of them, as if from one mouth, will set out more fully, in agreement with one another, what has been entrusted to them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the goads and nails as the precepts of the wise, handed on from one Shepherd.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: There is no profit in many words, and the conclusion is to fear God and keep His commandments, since every person will be judged and receive the recompense of his works.
comments.comment: There is no profit in many words (Ecclesiastes 12:12). Nor do I advise you, my friend, to write down useless things about what is fitting, in which there is nothing more than labor spent in vain (Ecclesiastes 12:12). It remains for me to add a conclusion such as this: O people, here I declare to you plainly and briefly: fear God, the Master and Overseer of all things, and keep His commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:13). And be persuaded that every person will afterward be judged, and that each will receive, as he deserves, the recompense of his own works, good and bad alike (Ecclesiastes 12:14).
comments.selected_reason: Reads the many books as useless writing and gives the book's conclusion: fear God and expect judgment.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
